cloud-operating-model.text: A deploy goes out at 16:50 on a Friday. Error rate climbs from 0.2% to 6%, the SLO burns, and three engineers start arguing about whether to roll back while customers see stale search results — because nobody agreed in advance what a bad deploy even looks like, or who pulls the cord.

The cloud operating model is the foundation lesson of Course 05: it is the contract that ties together containers, Kubernetes rollout, health checks, observability, and incident response into one repeatable loop. Everything downstream — canary, SLOs, runbooks — is an instance of this loop, so we build the loop first as a reviewable packet.

cloud-operating-model.prompt: Your deployment.yaml has readinessProbe and livenessProbe both pointing at GET /health, which returns 200 as soon as the process boots. The deploy goes 'green' in kubectl, but users get errors. What did the operating model get wrong? Answer before reading on.
cloud-operating-model.reveal: The health check lied. /health returned 200 before the service could actually serve traffic — DB pool not warm, index client not connected — so Kubernetes marked pods Ready and shifted live traffic onto them. 'Ready' must mean 'can serve a real request', not 'process is alive'. A liveness probe answers 'should I restart this?'; a readiness probe answers 'should I send traffic?' — conflating them turns your rollout gate into a rubber stamp, and a green kubectl rollout into a silent outage.

cloud-operating-model.intro: The operating model as config + the rollback transcript. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
cloud-operating-model.code:
# Rollout strategy: never replace all pods at once.
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }

# Readiness gate: 'Ready' must mean 'can serve a real request'.
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10 }

# Rollback trigger (the cord): error-rate SLO burns > 2% for 2 min.
# Proof of a safe reverse — captured live, pasted into the packet:
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index
Waiting for rollout: 2 of 4 updated replicas available...
error: deployment exceeded progress deadline   # bad image never went 100%
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/search-index
deployment.apps/search-index rolled back
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index
deployment "search-index" successfully rolled out   # last-good restored
steps: Rolling, never big-bang: maxUnavailable: 0 means old pods keep serving until new ones pass the gate. A bad image degrades a slice, not the whole service.
Readiness = serve, not boot: /readyz checks the DB pool and index client are actually connected. This is the gate the pretest's /health failed to be.
Liveness = restart, not traffic: /livez answers a different question: is the process wedged and worth killing? Conflating the two turns the rollout green while users get 500s.
The named trigger: The rollback cord is an SLO breach with a threshold and a window — not 'it feels bad'. This is the line that makes it an operating model.
The gate caught it: Because maxUnavailable was 0 and the gate was honest, the bad image hit the progress deadline instead of 100% of traffic.
The proven reverse: kubectl rollout undo restores the last-good ReplicaSet. This transcript IS the verification evidence the packet requires.

cloud-operating-model.subtitle: Push → CI → rolling deploy gated by the readiness probe → live traffic, watched by telemetry. The SLO breach is the decision: healthy continues; breach forces the rollback path. Payments and auth are out of scope.

legend.label: telemetry + the SLO that triggers rollback

storyboard.say: It starts with a git push. Your change gets built into an immutable image and stored in the registry, ready to ship.
The registry tag triggers a rolling deploy, replacing pods gradually instead of all at once so failure stays contained.
Here's the first gate: each new pod must pass its readiness probe before the deploy shifts traffic onto it.
Now it's live, serving real traffic and emitting metrics. But readiness only proves a pod started, not that the release is healthy.
Telemetry ties those metrics to an SLO. This is the decision point: error rate climbs 0.2% to 6% and the budget burns.
The SLO breach is the named trigger that pulls the cord, firing an automatic rollback nobody has to argue about at 16:50 on a Friday.
Rollback restores the last-good version to live service, closing the loop and returning error rates to baseline.
The invariant: every deploy has a reversal path proven before you need it. Rollout, an SLO to see it, and a trigger to undo it.

A reviewer reads the transcript and can name the process, its PID, and the port collision without you narrating.
linux-processes-ports.unlock: Your packet names the exact PID bound to the service port, the reason the new process could not bind, and the rollback command that restored health — all from real command output, not guesses.
linux-processes-ports.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'diagnosed the port issue' from `curl` failing or the container log alone. A 502 tells you the door is shut, not who is standing in it. Without ss/lsof output naming the PID that owns the socket, you have a symptom, not a diagnosis.

linux-processes-ports.text: The deploy went green in CI, but half of production is now returning 502s. The new pods keep crash-looping with 'address already in use', the VP is in the channel, and the only question that matters is one nobody has answered: which process is squatting on port 8080 — and is it safe to kill?

On Linux a running service is a process that holds a socket bound to a port; every deploy, rollback, health check, and incident ultimately grounds out in 'what is running and what is it listening on'. This lesson turns that into a reviewable incident packet — the same artifact the capstone reuses for its deployment drill.

linux-processes-ports.prompt: The container log says 'bind: address already in use' on port 8080. Your instinct is to restart the service again. Before you do — what does that error actually tell you about the machine? Answer first.
linux-processes-ports.reveal: It tells you a DIFFERENT process already owns that socket — restarting your service just loses the race again. The bind error is not about your app; it is about the OS refusing to hand the same port to two processes. The real move is `ss -ltnp | grep :8080` to name the current owner's PID, then decide: is it the old rollout that never exited, a zombie left by a failed deploy, or a second copy someone started by hand? You cannot fix a collision you have not identified.

linux-processes-ports.intro: Naming the port owner, one command at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
linux-processes-ports.code:
# 1. Who owns the service port right now?
$ ss -ltnp | grep ':8080'
LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("orders",pid=812,fd=7))

# 2. What IS pid 812? (the ps proves it is the OLD build)
$ ps -o pid,etime,cmd -p 812
  PID     ELAPSED CMD
  812    02:41:07 /app/orders --build=1.7.3   # started 2h ago = last rollout

# 3. Why can the NEW pod not start? (systemd/container log)
$ journalctl -u orders --since '5 min ago' | grep bind
orders[991]: FATAL: listen tcp :8080: bind: address already in use

# 4. Confirm nothing else is squatting (cross-check with lsof)
$ sudo lsof -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN
COMMAND PID   USER  FD  TYPE NODE NAME
orders  812  deploy   7u  IPv4      TCP *:8080 (LISTEN)

# 5. Roll back: stop the stuck old build, let the supervisor restart clean
$ sudo systemctl stop orders && sudo systemctl start orders
$ ss -ltnp | grep ':8080'
LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("orders",pid=1204,fd=7))  # fresh PID, healthy
steps: ss names the owner + PID: -l listening, -t tcp, -n numeric (no DNS stall), -p process. The PID in users:((...)) is the whole game — 812 owns the socket.
ps explains the PID: ELAPSED 02:41:07 and --build=1.7.3 prove this is the PREVIOUS rollout that never exited — not the new build. The PID is a name; ps gives it a story.
The log confirms the collision: The new process (PID 991) died on EADDRINUSE. Now the container error and the ss output tell one consistent story.
lsof cross-checks the owner: A second, independent tool confirming PID 812 owns :8080. Two tools agreeing is what turns a guess into evidence.
Roll back and re-verify: Stop the stuck process, let the supervisor rebind cleanly, then ss again — a NEW healthy PID (1204) now owns the port. Verification, not hope.
linux-processes-ports.commonMistake: No root cause, no evidence, will recur next deploy

linux-processes-ports.title: A port is owned by exactly one process; find the PID before you touch anything
linux-processes-ports.text: One socket, one owning process. The invariant: map port -> PID -> process before acting. `ss -ltnp` gives the listener and its PID; `ps` explains what that PID is; only then do you kill, roll back, or reconfigure. Guessing skips the map.

storyboard.say: Traffic enters through the load balancer, which fans every request at the single service socket on port 8080.
One socket has one owner. Right now port 8080 is held by the old rollout, PID 812, from the previous deploy.
The new rollout, PID 991, comes up and asks the Linux kernel to bind the same port with a bind() syscall.
The kernel refuses: the socket is taken, so it returns EADDRINUSE and PID 991 crash-loops instead of serving.
Because 812 never let go, traffic still lands on it, and the stale build keeps answering — that is the blast radius.
The fix is never a guess: map port to PID to process with ss -ltnp and ps before you kill anything.
The invariant to carry away: one socket, one owning process — resolve the owner first, then act.

linux-processes-ports.code:
# 1. Who owns the service port right now?
$ ss -ltnp | grep ':8080'
LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("orders",pid=812,fd=7))

# 2. What IS pid 812? (the ps proves it is the OLD build)
$ ps -o pid,etime,cmd -p 812
  PID     ELAPSED CMD
  812    02:41:07 /app/orders --build=1.7.3   # started 2h ago = last rollout

# 3. Why can the NEW pod not start? (systemd/container log)
$ journalctl -u orders --since '5 min ago' | grep bind
orders[991]: FATAL: listen tcp :8080: bind: address already in use

# 4. Confirm nothing else is squatting (cross-check with lsof)
$ sudo lsof -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN
COMMAND PID   USER  FD  TYPE NODE NAME
orders  812  deploy   7u  IPv4      TCP *:8080 (LISTEN)

# 5. Roll back: stop the stuck old build, let the supervisor restart clean
$ sudo systemctl stop orders && sudo systemctl start orders
$ ss -ltnp | grep ':8080'
LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:8080 0.0.0.0:* users:(("orders",pid=1204,fd=7))  # fresh PID, healthy

steps.label: ss names the owner + PID
steps.note: -l listening, -t tcp, -n numeric (no DNS stall), -p process. The PID in users:((...)) is the whole game — 812 owns the socket.

steps.label: ps explains the PID
steps.note: ELAPSED 02:41:07 and --build=1.7.3 prove this is the PREVIOUS rollout that never exited — not the new build. The PID is a name; ps gives it a story.

steps.label: The log confirms the collision
steps.note: The new process (PID 991) died on EADDRINUSE. Now the container error and the ss output tell one consistent story.

steps.label: lsof cross-checks the owner
steps.note: A second, independent tool confirming PID 812 owns :8080. Two tools agreeing is what turns a guess into evidence.

steps.label: Roll back and re-verify
steps.note: Stop the stuck process, let the supervisor rebind cleanly, then ss again — a NEW healthy PID (1204) now owns the port. Verification, not hope.

(DORA's framing is 'speed and stability are not tradeoffs' — the 'win on recovery, not on never breaking' is a fair gloss but 'evidence-backed' is the author's addition; DORA does not say elite teams win by recovering rather than avoiding failure.) The senior tell here is never `kill -9 <pid>` on a hunch — you `ss`/`lsof` to name the owner first, because killing the wrong PID during an incident is how a one-service blip becomes a multi-service outage. Identify, then act.

linux-processes-ports.question: The new rollout logs 'bind: address already in use' on port 8080. What is the FIRST command that actually moves the diagnosis forward?

environment-config-secrets.outcome: Take one deployable service and separate its configuration from its code: move every environment-specific value into env vars, route every secret through a real secret store (never a committed file), and write the config contract that a reviewer can audit — one artifact, no hardcoded credentials anywhere in the repo.
environment-config-secrets.proof: The `config` section of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md: a table of every config key (name, source, default, required?, secret?), proof that no secret is in the image or git history (a `git log -p | grep`-style scan returning clean), and the exact failure the app throws at boot when a required secret is absent. A reviewer confirms the same image runs in dev, staging, and prod with only env changes.
environment-config-secrets.unlock: Config lives outside the image, every secret comes from a secret store at runtime, and the app fails fast and loud when a required secret is missing.
environment-config-secrets.doNotClaim: Do not claim your config is externalized because you used a `.env` file. A `.env` committed to git — or baked into the Docker image — is a hardcoded secret with extra steps. Externalized means the same artifact carries NO environment values and NO credentials, and the secret is injected at runtime.

environment-config-secrets.text: A deploy goes out at 4:55 on a Friday, error rate spikes to 30%, and the on-call greps the logs to find `DATABASE_URL=postgres://admin:hunter2@prod-db` printed in plaintext — because the config was baked into the image and the staging password shipped to prod. One line of leaked config just became an incident and a credential rotation.

A container image is meant to be built once and run anywhere — dev, staging, prod — with only its environment changing. The moment a config value or secret is baked into the image, that promise breaks: you get environment drift, leaked credentials, and deploys that behave differently than the build you tested. This is the `config` section of the incident-repair packet you carry through this course.

environment-config-secrets.prompt: Your app needs a database password. Someone puts it in a `config.prod.json` file, commits it to the repo, and the CI pipeline copies it into the Docker image at build time. Name what is wrong before reading on — there is more than one thing.
environment-config-secrets.reveal: Three failures stacked. (1) The secret is in git history forever — rotating the DB password does not un-leak it; anyone who ever cloned the repo has it. (2) It is baked into the image, so the artifact you tested is now environment-specific — that same image cannot safely run in staging, breaking build-once-run-anywhere. (3) There is no fail-fast: a wrong or missing value is only discovered at runtime, mid-request, in production. The fix is not "use a different file" — it is inject config and secrets at runtime, from outside the image.

environment-config-secrets.intro: The 12-factor config module — validated, fail-fast, secret-safe. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
steps: Declare the contract: Every environment key is named in one schema. This IS the audit table a reviewer reads — non-secret config (NODE_ENV, PORT, LOG_LEVEL) can carry safe defaults.

Secrets have no defaults: DATABASE_URL and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY are required with NO default. A secret with a fallback default is a secret waiting to run against the wrong environment. `.startsWith('sk_')` catches a staging key shipped to prod.
Parse process.env, don't trust it: Config comes from the environment (injected by env vars + the secret store), validated at the boundary — never hardcoded, never read from a committed file.

Fail fast, fail loud: A missing or malformed secret exits at boot with the exact field that failed — the opposite of the 4:55-Friday incident where a bad value surfaced mid-request. This is the boot-time error your proof must show.

Freeze and never log: `Object.freeze` makes config immutable after boot; the schema never gets console-logged, so a secret cannot leak into your log stream — the exact plaintext-in-logs leak from the mission.

storyboard.say: It starts in the source repo. CI builds your code into one container image, meant to run unchanged in dev, staging, and prod.
Here is the leak. Someone commits a secret into the repo, so it gets baked in as a config value the build carries along.
That baked-in secret leaks straight into the artifact. Now the credential lives inside the image itself, and in git history forever.
Deploy that image per environment and the staging password rides into prod. On-call greps the logs and finds the DATABASE_URL in plaintext.
The fix, part one: build the image with zero environment values, then read config from env vars at boot.
Part two: pull secrets from a secret store at runtime, injected only into the container's memory, never into the image or repo.
The invariant: one image runs everywhere, config comes from env vars, secrets come from the store, and no credential ever exists in the artifact.

environment-config-secrets.title: The 12-factor config module — validated, fail-fast, secret-safe
environment-config-secrets.subtitle: The real Build artifact: load env at boot, require what must exist, crash loudly before serving a single request.

steps.label: Declare the contract
steps.note: Every environment key is named in one schema. This IS the audit table a reviewer reads — non-secret config (NODE_ENV, PORT, LOG_LEVEL) can carry safe defaults.

steps.label: Secrets have no defaults
steps.note: DATABASE_URL and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY are required with NO default. A secret with a fallback default is a secret waiting to run against the wrong environment. `.startsWith('sk_')` catches a staging key shipped to prod.

steps.label: Parse process.env, don't trust it
steps.note: Config comes from the environment (injected by env vars + the secret store), validated at the boundary — never hardcoded, never read from a committed file.

steps.label: Fail fast, fail loud
steps.note: A missing or malformed secret exits at boot with the exact field that failed — the opposite of the 4:55-Friday incident where a bad value surfaced mid-request. This is the boot-time error your proof must show.

steps.label: Freeze and never log
steps.note: `Object.freeze` makes config immutable after boot; the schema never gets console-logged, so a secret cannot leak into your log stream — the exact plaintext-in-logs leak from the mission.

environment-config-secrets.caption: Same image everywhere. `docker run -e DATABASE_URL=... -e STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=...` (from the secret store) is the ONLY thing that changes between dev, staging, and prod.

environment-config-secrets.title: Baked-in config vs externalized config
environment-config-secrets.subtitle: Same service, same secret. One ships the credential inside the artifact; one injects it at runtime.

left.label: Baked into the image
lines: Secret committed to git — in history forever
config.prod.json copied into the image at build
The tested artifact is now environment-specific
Wrong/missing value surfaces mid-request in prod
Rotating the password can't un-leak it
left.verdict: One leak becomes an incident + a rotation

right.label: Injected at runtime
lines: Zero env values or secrets in the image or repo
Config read from env vars at boot, validated
Secrets pulled from a store (Vault/K8s/SSM) at runtime
The same image runs in dev, staging, and prod
Missing required secret -> fail fast, loud, at boot
right.verdict: Build once, run anywhere, no leaks

environment-config-secrets.caption: Externalized means the artifact carries no environment values and no credentials — the secret is injected, never baked.

environment-config-secrets.text: The senior tell: rotation. Ask "if this credential leaked right now, how fast can we rotate it, and does the app pick up the new value without a rebuild?" If the secret is baked into the image, rotation means a full rebuild-and-redeploy of every service — minutes-to-hours of exposure. If it is injected from a secret store, rotation is a store update plus a pod restart — seconds. 12-factor exists to make that answer "seconds". (Twelve-Factor App is its own methodology by Adam Wiggins/Heroku; it is not authored or defined by DORA or SWEBOK — remove both attributions.)

environment-config-secrets.question: A reviewer says: "Prove this isn't just happy-path — show me the exact evidence your config is production-safe." Which single item is the strongest proof?
options: A screenshot of the app running fine locally with a `.env` file.
A `.env.example` file listing the variable names.
A boot log showing the app exit non-zero with the precise missing/invalid key when a required secret is absent, plus a clean git-history scan showing no secret was ever committed.
A comment in the Dockerfile saying "remember to set the secrets."
environment-config-secrets.explanation: The reviewer challenge from the source demands evidence, not vibes. A `.env.example` (2) documents names but proves nothing about behavior; a local run (1) is the happy path; a comment (4) is a hope. Only option 3 proves the two invariants that matter: the app fails fast and loud on a missing secret (the boot-time exit with the exact key), and no credential ever entered the artifact or git history (the clean scan). That is the auditable proof the incident-repair packet requires.

environment-config-secrets.intro: Prove your config is production-safe — no vibes:
items: Run the same image in two "environments" with only env vars changed. If it needs a rebuild to move from staging to prod, config is still baked in — externalize it.
Unset one required secret and boot. The app must exit non-zero and name the exact missing key. If it starts and fails later mid-request, your fail-fast is missing.

Scan git history for the secret's value pattern (e.g. `git log -p | grep -E 'sk_|postgres://.*:.*@'`). Any hit means the credential is leaked forever — rotate it and remove the source, not just the latest file.
Grep the built image (`docker history` / image layers) for credential patterns. A secret in a layer is a secret in the artifact.
Confirm no secret is ever logged: the config object is not console-dumped, and error messages print the KEY name, never the value.

prompts: Explain why committing a `.env` file to git is worse than it looks — what does rotation cost you, and why does deleting the file not fix it?
In your own words: what does "build once, run anywhere" require of your config, and how does injecting at runtime deliver it?
Why must a required secret have NO default value, using DATABASE_URL from your own config schema as the example?

container-image-design.outcome: Take one real service (or a realistic one) and design its container image: a multi-stage Dockerfile that produces a small, pinned, non-root, health-checkable image — then record why each layer earns its place in the deployment_incident_repair_packet.md.
container-image-design.proof: Section: "Image Design" of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md — a multi-stage Dockerfile with a pinned base digest, a builder stage separated from the runtime stage, a non-root USER, an ordered layer cache, and a HEALTHCHECK. A reviewer builds it and confirms the final image ships no compiler, no build cache, and no root shell as the default.
container-image-design.unlock: Your image is multi-stage, runs as non-root, pins its base by digest, and orders layers so a code change does not bust the dependency cache.
container-image-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim a "production image" because it runs locally. An image that runs as root, pins :latest, and bakes the build toolchain into the runtime layer runs fine on your laptop and is a supply-chain and rollback liability in production. Running is not the bar; reviewable is.

container-image-design.text: 3 a.m. page: a deploy pushed error rates past the SLO, and the on-call reaches for rollback — but the previous image was tagged :latest, so "the last good version" no longer resolves to anything. The image was never designed to be rolled back to.

In Cloud DevOps, the container image is the unit you ship, roll back, scan, and cache — every deploy, incident, and rollback runs through it. A well-designed image is small, reproducible, non-root, and pinned; a careless one is the root cause of the incident you are paged for.

container-image-design.prompt: Your Dockerfile ends with FROM node:latest and installs your whole toolchain into one layer. It builds and runs. Before you ship it — what is the production liability hiding in that image? Answer before reading on.
container-image-design.reveal: Three, actually. :latest means "the last good image" is unpinnable — rollback has no fixed target. One fat layer means every code change re-downloads every dependency, so builds and image pulls balloon. And baking the compiler + build cache into the runtime layer ships an attack surface you never run. It builds cleanly precisely because none of these fail at build time — they fail at 3 a.m., during a rollback, or in a security scan.

container-image-design.intro: Writing the Dockerfile, one decision at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
container-image-design.code:
# --- stage 1: builder (toolchain lives here, never ships) ---
FROM node:20.11-slim@sha256:2f...e9 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# --- stage 2: runtime (only what runs in production) ---
FROM node:20.11-slim@sha256:2f...e9 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist
USER node
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD node dist/healthcheck.js || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
steps: Pin the base by digest: sha256 digest, not :latest. Rollback needs a fixed target; a digest is the same bytes on every build, every machine, forever.
Deps before source: Copy the lockfile and install FIRST. This layer is cached; a code change downstream will not re-run npm ci — the single biggest build-speed lever.
Two stages, one toolchain: AS builder holds the compiler and build cache. The runtime stage starts fresh — none of that toolchain follows it into the shipped image.
Production deps only: --omit=dev drops test/build packages; cache clean removes the npm cache. Nothing here that you do not run in production.
Copy only the build output: COPY --from=builder pulls just /app/dist across the stage boundary. Source, node_modules-dev, and build cache stay behind.
Drop to non-root: USER node. If the process is compromised, the blast radius is a non-privileged user, not root inside the container.
Declare liveness: HEALTHCHECK lets the orchestrator distinguish live from wedged — the signal a rollout and a rollback both depend on.
container-image-design.commonMistake: Runs locally; a liability in prod

container-image-design.title: An image is a small, pinned, non-root, cache-ordered artifact — build stays out of runtime
container-image-design.text: Design the image so runtime carries only what runs: a multi-stage build discards the toolchain, a pinned base digest makes it reproducible, a non-root USER shrinks blast radius, and layer order keeps the dependency cache alive across code changes. The invariant: nothing in the runtime layer that you do not run in production.

#
# Mission: Take one real service (or a realistic one) and design its container image: a multi-stage Dockerfile that produces a small, pinned, non-root, health-checkable image — then record why each layer earns its place in the deployment_incident_repair_packet.md.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Inspect the final image: docker history shows no compiler, no build cache, and no dev dependencies in the runtime layer. If the toolchain is present, your stages leaked.
# 2. Confirm the base is pinned by @sha256 digest, not a mutable tag. Ask: could I redeploy this exact image next month and get identical bytes?
# 3. Run docker inspect (or check the Dockerfile): the default USER is non-root. If it is root, a container escape has more privilege than it needs.
# 4. Change one line of source and rebuild: the dependency-install layer must come from cache (CACHED), not re-run. If npm ci re-runs, your layer order is wrong.
# 5. Confirm a HEALTHCHECK exists and probes real liveness — so the orchestrator can tell a live pod from a wedged one during rollout and rollback.

# Local execution is practice feedback; it does not create controlled mastery evidence.

    ("COPY src/ ./src", "src-tree-51ec", 2, "builder"),

]

CHANGES = {"src-tree-51ec": "src-tree-9fb0"}

    raise NotImplementedError("complete the production decision")

simulate_rebuild(LAYERS, CHANGES)

container-image-design.title: The multi-stage image and its layer cache
container-image-design.subtitle: The builder stage (toolchain) is discarded; only dist crosses into the runtime stage. Deps-before-source keeps the cache alive when only code changes — the failure path (fat, root, :latest) is drawn muted and out.

legend.label: the toolchain kept OUT on purpose

storyboard.say: It's 3 a.m.: a deploy blew past the SLO and on-call wants rollback — but the last image was tagged :latest, so there's nothing to roll back to.
Design fixes this. Everything starts from a pinned base digest, so the build is reproducible byte-for-byte, not whatever :latest meant today.
Dependencies install as their own layer first. Because they sit below your source, editing code doesn't invalidate them — the dep cache stays warm.
The builder stage copies your source on top and compiles. This is where the heavy toolchain lives — compilers, dev headers, build junk.
The whole builder stage is discarded. Its toolchain never ships — that fat, root, :latest image is drawn out because it's the failure we refuse.
Only the built artifact crosses over: COPY --from=builder dist lands in a lean runtime stage carrying nothing you don't run in production.
That image pushes to the registry by digest, giving you an immutable, non-root, rollback-able unit. The invariant: runtime holds only what runs.

container-image-design.text: The senior tell is the digest, not the size. Elite performers restore service fast, and pinned, reproducible artifacts help make that possible — so rollback is "redeploy this exact sha256," not "rebuild and pray." If your rollback target is a mutable tag like :latest or :prod, you do not have a rollback; you have a rebuild with your fingers crossed. (DORA does not claim elite performers recover fast *because* deploys are pinned artifacts; DORA does not discuss reproducible/pinned artifacts at all — remove the causal DORA attribution.)

container-image-design.question: During an incident you must roll back to the last known-good image. Which image design makes that a safe, one-command operation?
options: The service is deployed by the tag :latest, which always points at the most recent build.
Each build is pushed and deployed by immutable digest (sha256), so the previous good version resolves to the exact same bytes.
The image is small, so it pulls quickly even if you rebuild it from source during the incident.
The Dockerfile runs as root, so it has permission to overwrite the running container in place.
container-image-design.explanation: Rollback needs a fixed, reproducible target. An immutable digest (option 2) means "the last good version" is the same bytes every time — no rebuild, no drift. :latest (1) is mutable and may already have moved. Fast pulls (3) and root (4) do not give you a stable thing to roll back TO — they are unrelated to whether the previous version is still addressable.

One compose.yaml would have made the whole stack a single command.

Before a service reaches CI, Kubernetes, or a rollout, it has to run somewhere reproducibly — with its store, queue, and dependencies wired together. Docker Compose is the foundation lesson of production operations: the local stack you can rebuild from one file is the same shape you later deploy, instrument, and roll back.

docker-compose-local-stack.prompt: Your app container starts, tries to connect to Postgres, and crashes with `connection refused`. You add `depends_on: [db]`. It still crashes intermittently. Why? Answer before reading on.
docker-compose-local-stack.reveal: `depends_on` only waits for the container to START, not for Postgres to be READY to accept connections. The container is up; the database inside it is still running startup and recovery. The fix is a health check on the db plus `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }` — order by readiness, never by "the process exists". Racing a slow dependency is the single most common local-stack failure.

docker-compose-local-stack.code:
services:
  app:
    build: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@db:5432/app
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
  cache:
    image: redis:7
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
volumes:
  pgdata:
steps: The service under development: `build: .` builds your app from the local Dockerfile, so the stack always runs the code in this repo — not a stale published image.
Wire dependencies by service NAME: `db` and `cache` are resolvable hostnames on the compose network. No IPs, no localhost — the network is the wiring.
Order by readiness, not start: `condition: service_healthy` is the fix for the pretest: the app is not started until Postgres AND Redis pass their health checks.

Persist state in a named volume: Without `pgdata`, every `down` wipes the database. The named volume makes data survive restarts — but a fresh `docker compose down -v` still gives a clean slate on demand.
The health check IS the contract: `pg_isready` returns non-zero until Postgres accepts connections. This is what `service_healthy` waits on — the readiness signal, not the process.
Cheap readiness for the cache too: `redis-cli ping` returns PONG only when Redis is serving. Every stateful dependency needs its own readiness probe, or the app races it.

storyboard.say: You run one command: docker compose up. This reads compose.yaml and builds the entire local stack — no hand-started containers, nothing undocumented.
The app service comes up needing two backends: a Postgres store and a Redis cache, all wired on one shared bridge network.
Postgres persists its data to a named pgdata volume, so state survives container restarts and rebuilds.
Here is the naive path: if compose only ordered by start, the app boots the instant the DB container starts — but before it can accept connections.
That race is the classic works-on-my-machine failure: the app connects too early and gets connection refused from a database that isn't ready.
The fix is depends_on with service_healthy. The app waits until Postgres and Redis pass their health checks, not merely until they've started.
That's the invariant: one file, one command rebuilds the whole world — stores, cache, network, and startup order — and nothing reaches outside it.

options: Add a `sleep 10` to the app's entrypoint so Postgres has time to start.
Add a health check to Postgres and gate the app with `depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }`.

networking-dns-tls.outcome: Take one service that must be reachable over HTTPS through Kubernetes (Service → Ingress → DNS → TLS) and produce a deployment_incident_repair_packet.md that traces a real name-resolution or certificate failure end to end, names the blast radius, picks a rollback vs. re-issue decision, and proves the fix with a kubectl transcript and a curl TLS handshake.
networking-dns-tls.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md with: the request path (client → DNS → ingress → service → pod), the exact broken hop, a kubectl transcript, an openssl/curl handshake showing the cert chain resolving, the rollback-vs-reissue decision with a reversal condition, and a reviewer objection answered. A peer can point at the packet and say which hop failed and how you proved it healed.
networking-dns-tls.unlock: Your packet names the failing hop (DNS record, Service selector, Ingress host, or TLS cert), shows the blast radius, and proves resolution with a real handshake transcript — not a screenshot of a green dashboard.
networking-dns-tls.doNotClaim: Do not claim the service is 'up' because the pod is Running. A Running pod with a broken Service selector, a missing DNS record, or an expired cert is still a total outage to the user. 'Reachable' means a real client completed a TLS handshake to the right name and got a 200 — prove that hop, not pod health.

networking-dns-tls.text: 3 a.m. page: the API is 'down.' Every pod is Running, CPU is flat, logs are clean — and yet every browser shows NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID. The cert renewed to a name nobody pointed DNS at. The service was never down; the path to it was.

In production, a service is only as reachable as the chain in front of it: DNS resolves the name, the Ingress terminates TLS and routes the host, the Service load-balances to healthy pods. This lesson makes that chain inspectable so an incident becomes 'which hop broke' instead of 'everything is on fire.'

networking-dns-tls.prompt: Users report your site is unreachable. `kubectl get pods` shows every pod Running and Ready. Where do you look first — the pods, or somewhere else? Decide before reading.
networking-dns-tls.reveal: Not the pods. Ready pods mean the workload is healthy; it says nothing about whether traffic can reach them. The failure lives in the path: a stale DNS A/CNAME record, an Ingress host that no longer matches, a Service selector that stopped matching pod labels, or a TLS cert that expired or was issued for the wrong SNI. The 'oh!' — pod health and reachability are different axes, and 90% of 'the service is down' pages are actually 'the path to the service broke.'

networking-dns-tls.intro: The manifest that wires the whole path — and the openssl proof. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
networking-dns-tls.code:
# Ingress: host + TLS secret
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: api
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: ["api.example.com"]      # must match cert SAN + DNS record
      secretName: api-tls             # Secret cert-manager fills
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com           # must equal tls.hosts[0]
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: api-svc, port: { number: 80 } }
---
# Service: selector must match the pods' labels, or endpoints is empty
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: api-svc }
spec:
  selector: { app: api }              # pods carry label app=api
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]

# PROOF (paste transcript into the packet):
#   kubectl get endpoints api-svc        -> ADDRESSES must be non-empty
#   dig +short api.example.com           -> must return the LB IP
#   openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com 2>/dev/null \
#     | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates   -> subject=CN api.example.com, notAfter in the future
steps: One name, three places: tls.hosts, rules.host, and the DNS record must be the identical string. A typo or a renamed host silently 404s or fails SNI — the pod never sees the request.

The TLS Secret: cert-manager writes the cert+key into secretName. If issuance failed (rate limit, DNS-01 challenge unmet), this Secret is stale or missing and the Ingress serves an expired or default cert.

The selector is the silent killer: selector app=api must match the pods' labels exactly. A label drift (app=api-v2 on new pods) empties the endpoints list — Service resolves, routes nowhere, 503s. Healthy pods, zero reachability.
Endpoints is the fast disqualifier: Empty ADDRESSES = selector/label mismatch, not a DNS or TLS problem. This one command eliminates a whole branch in seconds.
dig proves the DNS hop: If dig returns the wrong IP or NXDOMAIN, the request never reaches your cluster — stop debugging Kubernetes and fix the record.

The handshake is the real proof: openssl s_client with -servername forces SNI. subject + notAfter prove the RIGHT cert for the RIGHT name is live and unexpired. This transcript is the packet's proof, not a green dashboard.
networking-dns-tls.commonMistake: Restarted healthy pods; the expired cert is still live

The invariant: every hop must agree on the same name and labels. One mismatch anywhere is a total outage, even with perfectly healthy pods.

networking-dns-tls.title: The request path — where DNS and TLS actually break
networking-dns-tls.subtitle: Client resolves the name, hits the Ingress (TLS terminates here), which routes by host to a Service, which selects pods by label. Two suspect edges are marked: the DNS record and the TLS cert. The pods themselves are healthy and out of the blast path.

legend.label: suspect edges: DNS record + TLS cert

storyboard.say: It's 3 a.m. Every browser shows a cert error, yet every pod is Running. The service was never down — the path to it broke.
The request starts at the Client, which first asks DNS to resolve the name into an address it can actually connect to.
DNS hands back an IP, and the client connects to the Ingress load balancer sitting at that address.
At the Ingress, TLS terminates. The server presents its cert chain for the requested name via SNI — this is where the invalid-cert error fires.
If the cert clears, the Ingress routes by host header to the matching Service — the internal entry point for that name.
The Service uses its label selector to pick healthy Pods and load-balances across them. The pods here are fine and out of the blast path.
The two suspect edges are the DNS record and the cert. One name mismatch anywhere is a total outage — even with perfectly healthy pods.

networking-dns-tls.question: Reviewer challenge: your users get 503s. Every pod is Running and Ready, `dig` returns the correct IP, and the TLS handshake succeeds with a valid, unexpired cert. Which is the most likely failing hop — and what proves it?
options: The pods are unhealthy; restart the deployment to be safe.
The Service selector no longer matches the pods' labels, so the endpoints list is empty — `kubectl get endpoints api-svc` returns no ADDRESSES.
DNS is stale; flush the resolver cache and wait for TTL.
The TLS certificate expired; re-issue it via cert-manager.
networking-dns-tls.explanation: DNS is proven good (dig correct) and TLS is proven good (handshake + unexpired cert), so those hops are eliminated. Ready pods mean the workload is fine. A 503 with a healthy pod and a completed handshake points to routing: the Service resolved but has no endpoints because its selector stopped matching the pod labels. `kubectl get endpoints` returning empty ADDRESSES is the falsifiable proof. Options 3 and 4 were already disqualified by evidence; 1 restarts healthy pods and fixes nothing.

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) deployable service and add a CI pipeline quality gate: a stage that BLOCKS a bad build from reaching production on a falsifiable, machine-checked threshold — not a human's opinion. Package the evidence as deployment_incident_repair_packet.md.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md plus the gate config (a real CI stage: tests + coverage floor + a security or contract check) with a transcript showing the pipeline PASS on a good commit and FAIL-CLOSED on a seeded bad commit. A reviewer can point to the exact line where the gate refused to promote the artifact.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.unlock: Your gate fails the pipeline (non-zero exit, no promotion) on a real defect, and you can show the transcript where it did.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a quality gate if the check runs but never blocks the merge or deploy — a gate that only warns is a linter with anxiety. If a failing check still lets the artifact promote, it is theater, not a gate. The invariant: a red gate stops the release.

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.text: 3:40 p.m. Friday: a green checkmark on the PR, a deploy to prod, and within ninety seconds the error rate quadruples — because 'green' only meant the code compiled. The tests that would have caught it existed, but nothing in the pipeline was allowed to say no.

A CI pipeline quality gate is the smallest place where 'we should test this' becomes 'this cannot ship untested' — enforced by the machine, not remembered by a human. Change-failure rate is a genuine DORA metric, but DORA does not frame any specific 'control' as turning it 'from luck into policy' — that framing is the author's, not DORA's. Rewrite as: 'It is the control that improves your change-failure rate (a DORA metric) from luck into policy, and it is the evidence a reviewer trusts before they trust your service.'

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.prompt: Your CI runs the full test suite on every push, and the results show up right in the PR. Is that a quality gate? Answer before reading on.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.reveal: Not yet. Running a check and ENFORCING it are different axes. If the merge button is still clickable while tests are red — or the deploy job runs regardless of the test job's result — you have observability, not a gate. A gate is a required status that fails CLOSED: the pipeline exits non-zero, the artifact is never promoted, and no human can wave it through without an explicit, logged override. 'Tests ran' is a fact; 'tests must pass to ship' is a gate.

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.intro: Building the gate, one stage at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.code:
name: quality-gate
on: [pull_request, push]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Unit + integration tests
        run: pytest --maxfail=1 --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing
      - name: Enforce coverage floor
        run: coverage report --fail-under=80
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t app:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Scan image for critical CVEs
        run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL app:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    needs: gate            # <- deploy CANNOT run unless gate is green
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Rollout
        run: kubectl set image deploy/app app=app:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Wait for healthy rollout
        run: kubectl rollout status deploy/app --timeout=120s
steps: Tests as a hard step: --maxfail=1 stops on the first real failure. This step's non-zero exit is what makes the whole job red — nothing downstream runs.
The coverage floor: --fail-under=80 turns 'we have tests' into 'we have ENOUGH tests'. A falsifiable threshold, not a vibe: 79.9% exits non-zero.
Security is part of the gate: trivy --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL fails the build on a critical CVE in the image. Security is a gate stage, not a separate quarterly ritual.

needs: gate — the load-bearing line: This single dependency is what makes it a GATE. Without it, deploy runs in parallel and ships regardless of test results. With it, red gate = no deploy, by construction.

Rollout is verified, not fired-and-forgotten: kubectl rollout status --timeout=120s means the pipeline only reports success once the new pods are actually healthy — closing the loop the mission opened.

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.title: A gate fails closed on a falsifiable threshold and blocks promotion

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.subtitle: A commit flows left to right. The gate is the one decision node that can send an artifact to quarantine instead of prod — and it shows both the pass path and the fail-closed repair path.

legend.label: the gate — the one node that can say no

storyboard.say: It starts with a commit or PR. That's the entry point — a change that wants to reach production.
The commit triggers a build. The artifact gets compiled and packaged, then handed forward for inspection.
The artifact flows into the quality gate — the one decision node that decides whether this change is allowed to proceed.
On pass — tests green, coverage above floor, no criticals — the gate promotes the artifact into the registry, then it rolls out to prod.
On fail, the gate exits non-zero and routes the artifact to quarantine. Red means no ship — no silent override to prod.
Quarantine captures the evidence into a repair packet, so the failure comes with the context needed to fix it.
The repair packet loops back to a new commit that fixes and re-runs. The gate is the smallest place where 'should test' becomes 'cannot ship untested.'

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.title: Building the gate, one stage at a time
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.subtitle: A GitHub Actions job that fails closed: tests, a coverage floor, and a container CVE scan — each able to stop the deploy.
ci-pipeline-quality-gates.code:
name: quality-gate
on: [pull_request, push]

jobs:
  gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Unit + integration tests
        run: pytest --maxfail=1 --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing
      - name: Enforce coverage floor
        run: coverage report --fail-under=80
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t app:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Scan image for critical CVEs
        run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL app:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    needs: gate            # <- deploy CANNOT run unless gate is green
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Rollout
        run: kubectl set image deploy/app app=app:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Wait for healthy rollout
        run: kubectl rollout status deploy/app --timeout=120s

steps.label: Tests as a hard step
steps.note: --maxfail=1 stops on the first real failure. This step's non-zero exit is what makes the whole job red — nothing downstream runs.

steps.label: The coverage floor
steps.note: --fail-under=80 turns 'we have tests' into 'we have ENOUGH tests'. A falsifiable threshold, not a vibe: 79.9% exits non-zero.

steps.label: Security is part of the gate
steps.note: trivy --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL fails the build on a critical CVE in the image. Security is a gate stage, not a separate quarterly ritual.

steps.label: needs: gate — the load-bearing line
steps.note: This single dependency is what makes it a GATE. Without it, deploy runs in parallel and ships regardless of test results. With it, red gate = no deploy, by construction.

steps.label: Rollout is verified, not fired-and-forgotten
steps.note: kubectl rollout status --timeout=120s means the pipeline only reports success once the new pods are actually healthy — closing the loop the mission opened.

ci-pipeline-quality-gates.text: DORA does not 'make explicit' any statement about what makes a good gate; it measures delivery outcomes, not gate design. Rewrite as: 'The senior move: a good gate is FAST and TRUSTWORTHY, not just strict.' A gate that takes 40 minutes or fails randomly (flaky tests) trains engineers to bypass it — and a routinely-overridden gate is worse than none, because it launders bad ships as 'reviewed'. Quarantine flakes, keep the gate under ~10 minutes, and make every override an explicit, logged decision. A gate people trust is a gate people obey.

options: A screenshot of the pipeline passing green on a clean commit.
A CI transcript on a SEEDED bad commit showing the gate step exit non-zero, the deploy job skipped with 'needs: gate' unmet, and the merge blocked — captured in the repair packet.
A slide saying 'we run tests on every push'.
A high coverage number printed in the logs.

A green run (1), a claim (3), or a metric with no enforcement (4) never show the gate refusing to promote — which is the entire skill.

artifact-versioning-releases.outcome: Take one deployable service and give it a real release identity: an immutable, content-addressed artifact tagged with a semantic version, promoted (not rebuilt) across environments, with a rollback target that is a prior artifact digest — not a re-run of the pipeline. Then write the release evidence into deployment_incident_repair_packet.md.
artifact-versioning-releases.proof: Section 'Release Identity' of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md: the artifact name + immutable digest (e.g. sha256:…), the semver tag, the environments it was promoted through, and the exact prior digest you would roll back to. A reviewer can point kubectl at the rollback digest without waiting for a rebuild.
artifact-versioning-releases.unlock: Your release names an immutable digest, a semver tag, a promote-not-rebuild path, and a concrete rollback target artifact.
artifact-versioning-releases.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'versioned the release' if your rollback plan is 'redeploy from main' or 'rebuild the last tag'. Rebuilding is a NEW artifact with new dependencies — it is not the thing that was running. If your rollback target is a branch or a re-run instead of a pinned digest, you have a version label, not a release you can restore.

artifact-versioning-releases.text: 2 a.m., checkout error rate is climbing past the SLO, and the on-call types 'roll it back' — but the tag :latest now points at the bad build, the last green image was garbage-collected, and rebuilding from the old commit pulls a patched base image that behaves differently. The rollback that should take ninety seconds turns into a forty-minute rebuild while customers can't pay.

A release is the unit you deploy, promote, and reverse — and it is only trustworthy if it is immutable and identifiable. Artifact versioning turns 'the code from last Tuesday' into a content-addressed thing with a known digest, so rollout, rollback, and incident forensics all point at the same object instead of guessing.

artifact-versioning-releases.prompt: Your deploy uses the container tag myapp:latest. You push a fix, CI builds, prod pulls myapp:latest. What's the failure mode hiding in that one word — before you read on?
artifact-versioning-releases.reveal: A tag is a mutable pointer, not a version. myapp:latest today and myapp:latest tonight can be two different images with different layers, because :latest just re-points to whatever was pushed last. Two nodes pulling 'the same' tag at different times run different code, rollback has no fixed target, and your incident log says 'we deployed latest' — which is unfalsifiable. The fix isn't a better tag name; it's pinning to the immutable digest (sha256:…) that names the exact bytes, and letting the semver tag be a friendly alias on top of it.

artifact-versioning-releases.intro: Cutting and pinning the release, one command at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
artifact-versioning-releases.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

VERSION="v2.4.1"                          # semantic version = the human-facing name
GIT_SHA="$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"   # provenance: which commit produced this
REPO="registry.example.com/checkout"

# 1. Build ONCE. Stamp version + commit into the image as provenance labels.
docker build \
  --label "org.opencontainers.image.version=${VERSION}" \
  --label "org.opencontainers.image.revision=${GIT_SHA}" \
  -t "${REPO}:${VERSION}" .

# 2. Push, then capture the IMMUTABLE digest the registry assigns.
docker push "${REPO}:${VERSION}"
DIGEST="$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "${REPO}:${VERSION}")"
echo "pinned release: ${DIGEST}"          # e.g. registry.example.com/checkout@sha256:ab12...

# 3. Promote the SAME digest across envs — never rebuild per stage.
kubectl -n staging set image deploy/checkout app="${DIGEST}"
kubectl -n prod    set image deploy/checkout app="${DIGEST}"
kubectl -n prod    rollout status deploy/checkout --timeout=120s

# 4. Rollback target is a PRIOR digest, retained in the registry — not a rebuild.
PREV_DIGEST="registry.example.com/checkout@sha256:90ff..."   # v2.4.0, still pinned
# kubectl -n prod set image deploy/checkout app="${PREV_DIGEST}"   # 90s restore, byte-identical
steps: Name the release + its provenance: Semver is the friendly alias; the git SHA records exactly which commit produced these bytes. Both get stamped into the artifact so forensics can trace it later.

Build ONCE with OCI provenance labels: org.opencontainers.image.version + .revision are the standard labels every scanner and registry reads. Build here, not per environment — a per-stage rebuild is a different artifact.
Capture the immutable digest: RepoDigests gives you registry/repo@sha256:… — the content-addressed identity. This, not :v2.4.1, is what you pin. The tag can be re-pointed; the digest cannot.
Promote the same digest across envs: set image with the @sha256 reference guarantees staging and prod run byte-identical bytes. This is 'promote, don't rebuild' made literal.
Gate on rollout status: rollout status with a timeout turns the promotion into a verifiable step — it succeeds only when the new pods are healthy, or the pipeline fails loudly.

Pin the rollback target: The prior digest is retained (never garbage-collect the last N releases). Rollback is one set image to a known digest — a 90-second restore of the exact bytes that were green, not a 40-minute rebuild.

artifact-versioning-releases.subtitle: One immutable artifact (sha256:ab12…) flows staging → canary → prod. The bad release v2.4.1 crossed the SLO; rollback re-points prod at the prior pinned digest v2.4.0 — no rebuild. Analytics reads the same registry, so forensics agree on one object.

legend.label: the one artifact, built once and promoted
the bad release + SLO breach (failure path)
immutable registry + pinned rollback target (repair path)

storyboard.say: CI builds the code once into a single immutable artifact and pushes it to the registry, addressed by its sha256 digest.
That exact digest is pulled into staging — not rebuilt, promoted. What you test is the literal bytes that shipped.
The same digest advances to canary, then to prod — one object walking the pipeline, never a fresh build per stage.
Prod emits its error rate to the SLO monitor — the release v2.4.1 crosses the threshold and trips the breach.
On breach, rollback targets the prior release v2.4.0 — still retained in the registry by its own pinned digest.
Prod re-points at that pinned prior digest — no rebuild, no patched base image, just the last known-good bytes back in seconds.
The invariant: tested, shipped, and rolled-back-to are the same immutable object — so rollout, rollback, and forensics never guess.

artifact-versioning-releases.title: Cutting and pinning the release, one command at a time
artifact-versioning-releases.subtitle: Build once, capture the digest, tag semver, promote by digest, roll back by digest. The digest — not the tag — is the identity.
artifact-versioning-releases.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

VERSION="v2.4.1"                          # semantic version = the human-facing name
GIT_SHA="$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"   # provenance: which commit produced this
REPO="registry.example.com/checkout"

# 1. Build ONCE. Stamp version + commit into the image as provenance labels.
docker build \
  --label "org.opencontainers.image.version=${VERSION}" \
  --label "org.opencontainers.image.revision=${GIT_SHA}" \
  -t "${REPO}:${VERSION}" .

# 2. Push, then capture the IMMUTABLE digest the registry assigns.
docker push "${REPO}:${VERSION}"
DIGEST="$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "${REPO}:${VERSION}")"
echo "pinned release: ${DIGEST}"          # e.g. registry.example.com/checkout@sha256:ab12...

# 3. Promote the SAME digest across envs — never rebuild per stage.
kubectl -n staging set image deploy/checkout app="${DIGEST}"
kubectl -n prod    set image deploy/checkout app="${DIGEST}"
kubectl -n prod    rollout status deploy/checkout --timeout=120s

# 4. Rollback target is a PRIOR digest, retained in the registry — not a rebuild.
PREV_DIGEST="registry.example.com/checkout@sha256:90ff..."   # v2.4.0, still pinned
# kubectl -n prod set image deploy/checkout app="${PREV_DIGEST}"   # 90s restore, byte-identical

steps.label: Name the release + its provenance
steps.note: Semver is the friendly alias; the git SHA records exactly which commit produced these bytes. Both get stamped into the artifact so forensics can trace it later.

steps.label: Build ONCE with OCI provenance labels
steps.note: org.opencontainers.image.version + .revision are the standard labels every scanner and registry reads. Build here, not per environment — a per-stage rebuild is a different artifact.

steps.label: Capture the immutable digest
steps.note: RepoDigests gives you registry/repo@sha256:… — the content-addressed identity. This, not :v2.4.1, is what you pin. The tag can be re-pointed; the digest cannot.

steps.label: Promote the same digest across envs
steps.note: set image with the @sha256 reference guarantees staging and prod run byte-identical bytes. This is 'promote, don't rebuild' made literal.

steps.label: Gate on rollout status
steps.note: rollout status with a timeout turns the promotion into a verifiable step — it succeeds only when the new pods are healthy, or the pipeline fails loudly.

steps.label: Pin the rollback target
steps.note: The prior digest is retained (never garbage-collect the last N releases). Rollback is one set image to a known digest — a 90-second restore of the exact bytes that were green, not a 40-minute rebuild.

artifact-versioning-releases.text: The senior tell isn't the semver scheme — it's provenance plus retention. DORA measures fast time-to-restore (failed-deployment recovery time) but does not attribute it to 'a prior good artifact still existing and being addressable' — that causal mechanism is not DORA's claim. Rewrite as: 'DORA's elite performers are defined partly by fast service restoration (failed-deployment recovery time); a practical way to get there is keeping a prior good artifact addressable — and SWEBOK's configuration-management discipline says the build should be reproducible and identifiable, not re-derived.' If you can't name the digest of what's running in prod right now, and prove where it came from, you don't have a release — you have a deployment you're hoping stays up.

deployment-strategies.text: Friday, 4:58 p.m. You ship a new search-index build to production. Within ninety seconds the 5xx rate triples and orders start failing — and the only question that matters is whether your deploy stops itself at 5% of traffic or takes down 100% of customers before anyone opens Slack.

A deployment strategy is how new code replaces old code in production without a full-blast outage: rolling, blue-green, or canary, each trading speed against blast radius and reversibility. This lesson turns that choice into a reviewable packet with a health gate and a rollback trigger — the artifact you carry into the incident drill and readiness review.

deployment-strategies.prompt: "We'll deploy the new version to all pods at once — it passed staging, so it's fine." Before you argue about pod counts — what is wrong with that as a deployment strategy? Answer before reading on.
deployment-strategies.reveal: Staging is not production traffic, and 'all at once' gives you nowhere to stand when it fails. The bug that survives staging is the one that only appears under real load, real data, or real concurrency — exactly the conditions you skipped. A strategy is not 'how do I get the new bits out'; it is 'how do I limit who gets hurt while I find out if the new bits are safe'. All-at-once answers the first question and ignores the second, which is the only one that saves you at 4:58 on a Friday.

# Strategy: canary via rolling update, maxSurge=1 maxUnavailable=0, gated on readiness
$ kubectl set image deploy/search-index app=search-index:v2 --record
deployment.apps/search-index image updated

$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index --timeout=120s
Waiting for rollout: 1 of 4 updated replicas are available...
Waiting for rollout: 2 of 4 updated replicas are available...

# Health gate: SLO watcher fires — 5xx on canary pods at 3.2% (SLO = <1%)
$ kubectl logs deploy/search-index -l version=v2 --tail=3
ERROR upstream connect timeout: postgres pool exhausted (v2 raised pool from 10->2)

# Rollback trigger hit: error-rate > 1% for 2 min -> reverse to known-good
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/search-index
deployment.apps/search-index rolled back

$ kubectl rollout status deploy/search-index
deployment "search-index" successfully rolled out   # 5xx back to 0.1%
steps: Name the strategy + its safety knobs: maxUnavailable=0 means old pods stay serving until new ones pass readiness — the rollout never drops below capacity.
Trigger the rollout, recorded: --record writes the change into rollout history so `undo` has a known-good revision to return to. Reversibility is set up BEFORE the risk.

Gate on rollout status: Do not fire-and-forget. `rollout status` blocks until pods are Available (readiness-probe green) or the timeout trips — this is the health gate, not a dashboard you hope someone watches.

The health signal turns red: The canary's own logs show the cause: v2 shrank the Postgres pool, so under real traffic connections exhaust. This only appears in production load — exactly what canary exists to catch at 5%, not 100%.
Rollback trigger fires: error-rate > 1% for 2 min crosses the SLO threshold. `rollout undo` reverses to the recorded known-good revision — no code fix, no redeploy, just restore.
Prove the reversal worked: Confirm 5xx returns to baseline. The incident is contained to the ~5% canary window; the packet attaches this transcript as proof.

legend.label: canary — small blast radius under test

storyboard.say: It's 4:58 Friday and you ship. All live requests still arrive at one front door: the traffic split router.
Canary is the safety choice: the router keeps 95% of traffic on the proven v1 stable version.
Only 5% of traffic touches the new v2 canary — so a bad build's blast radius starts small, not global.
The canary emits live metrics; the SLO watcher reads them as the health signal that gates the rollout forward.
If the canary stays green with error rate under 1%, the watcher promotes it to 100% of traffic.
But errors triple: over 1% for two minutes trips the burn trigger, so the watcher halts and calls rollback.
Rollback restores the known-good v1, and traffic reverts to stable — automatically, before anyone opens Slack.
The invariant: a bad version must halt and reverse on measurable evidence before it reaches all users.

deployment-strategies.caption: The strategy is not the deploy command — it is the halt condition. Canary without an automatic gate is just a slower big-bang.

deployment-strategies.text: Standards grounding: DORA's four keys measure exactly this — deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, and time-to-restore. A canary with an SLO gate is how elite teams keep change-failure rate low AND restore-time in minutes at the same time. The senior tell: they can state the rollback trigger as a number ('err-rate > 1% for 2 min') before they run the deploy, not discover it during the incident.

deployment-strategies.question: Reviewer challenge: which deployment plan actually limits blast radius and is reversible on evidence?
options: "Roll it out to all pods at once — it passed staging and CI is green."
"Canary at 5% behind a traffic split, promote only when 5xx stays under 1% for 5 min, and auto-rollback via `rollout undo` if error-rate exceeds 1% for 2 min."
"Deploy Friday evening when traffic is low so fewer people notice if it breaks."
"Blue-green cutover with no health check on green — just flip the router once the new pods start."
deployment-strategies.explanation: Only option 2 has both halves of a real strategy: a bounded blast radius (5% behind a split) and an automatic halt tied to a measurable SLO (rollback on err > 1% / 2 min). Option 1 ships to 100% with no gate; option 3 confuses low traffic with safety and has no rollback trigger; option 4 is blue-green in name only — flipping to an unhealthed green is a big-bang with extra steps.

deployment-strategies.intro: Prove your deployment packet holds — no happy-path:

There is a real rollout transcript (kubectl rollout status or equivalent), not a description of one. If you have no command output, you have a plan, not proof.
A health gate exists that can HALT the rollout automatically: a readiness probe plus an SLO signal, not 'someone watches the dashboard'.
The rollback trigger is a number, not a vibe: name the metric, the threshold, and the duration (e.g. 5xx > 1% for 2 min), and show the reversal command returns to a known-good revision.
The blast radius is named and bounded: what breaks, for what fraction of traffic, and whether it is degraded vs data-loss — stale search ≠ lost orders.

health-readiness-liveness.proof: The `probes` section of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md: a Deployment manifest with startupProbe, readinessProbe, and livenessProbe that check different things (process-up vs dependency-ready vs deadlock-detect), PLUS a kubectl rollout transcript showing an unready pod pulled from the Service endpoints WITHOUT being restarted. A reviewer confirms readiness and liveness are not the same check with two names.
health-readiness-liveness.unlock: Your three probes each answer a distinct question, and you can show a pod going NotReady (drained from Service) without being killed — proving readiness ≠ liveness.
health-readiness-liveness.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'added health checks' if your readiness and liveness probes hit the same endpoint. That is one check wearing two hats: a slow dependency will fail liveness, restart the pod, drop its warm cache, and make the incident WORSE. Different probes must answer different questions.

health-readiness-liveness.text: A deploy goes out at 4:55pm. The new pods pass their single `/health` check the instant the process starts — so Kubernetes sends them live traffic before the DB pool is warm, and every one of them returns 503s to real customers for ninety seconds. The liveness check was green the whole time. Nobody had told the cluster the difference between 'alive' and 'ready to serve.'

Kubernetes cannot see inside your container; probes are the only language it has for 'is this pod alive, and should it get traffic?' Get the two confused and the platform will either route requests into a cold pod or restart a healthy-but-busy one — the difference between a smooth rollout and a self-inflicted outage.

health-readiness-liveness.prompt: Your pod's database connection drops for 20 seconds. Should Kubernetes (a) restart the pod, or (b) stop sending it traffic but leave it running? Decide before reading on.
health-readiness-liveness.reveal: Stop sending traffic — do NOT restart. A dropped dependency is a READINESS failure: the pod is alive and may reconnect in seconds, so you want it pulled from the load balancer, not killed. Restarting throws away its warm connection pool and in-flight work, and if the DB is the real problem, a restart storm across every pod makes recovery slower. Liveness is only for 'this process is wedged and will never recover on its own' — a deadlock, not a hiccup. Wiring a dependency check into liveness is the classic way to turn a 20-second blip into a cascading restart loop.

health-readiness-liveness.intro: The three-probe Deployment, line by line. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
health-readiness-liveness.code:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: orders-api
    image: orders-api:1.8.2
    ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
    startupProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 2          # allow up to 60s to boot
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }   # checks DB pool + migrations
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 2       # 2 misses → drain from Service
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }   # process/event-loop only
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 3       # 3 misses → restart (real hang)
steps: startupProbe gates the rest: 30 × 2s = up to 60s to finish booting. Until it passes, readiness and liveness are DISABLED — so a slow migration on cold start can't be misread as a deadlock and trigger a restart loop.
readinessProbe = can I serve?: /readyz checks the DB pool and that migrations ran. failureThreshold: 2 keeps a single blip from flapping the pod out. Failing drains traffic — the pod stays alive.
Different endpoint on purpose: /readyz (dependency-aware) must NOT be the same path as liveness. If liveness also checked the DB, a DB hiccup would restart every pod at once.
livenessProbe = am I wedged?: /healthz answers only 'is the process responsive?' — no downstream calls. failureThreshold: 3 (30s) means a restart fires only for a genuine hang, not a busy moment.

health-readiness-liveness.title: Three probes, three different questions
health-readiness-liveness.text: Startup asks 'has it finished booting?' — it gates the other two so a slow start is not mistaken for a hang. Readiness asks 'can it serve a request right now?' — failing drains traffic. Liveness asks 'is it permanently stuck?' — failing restarts. The invariant: readiness drains, liveness restarts, and they must check different things.

legend.label: readiness path — drains traffic, pod lives

storyboard.say: It starts with the kubelet: the only thing outside your container asking, in three separate questions, whether this pod is alive and should get traffic.
First the kubelet runs the startupProbe, which gates the other two so a slow boot is never mistaken for a hang.
Only once startup succeeds does the kubelet enable readiness and liveness — nothing routes traffic or restarts before boot completes.
readinessProbe asks 'can it serve right now?' — pass, and the pod stays in the Service endpoints taking live traffic.
Fail readiness and the pod is REMOVED from endpoints — traffic drains away, but the pod survives to recover.
livenessProbe asks a different question: 'is it permanently stuck?' — fail, and the kubelet kills and restarts the container.
The 4:55 outage: a single /health check went green at process start, so cold pods got traffic. Readiness drains, liveness restarts — check different things.

kubernetes-manifests.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'wrote Kubernetes manifests' if your Deployment has no readiness probe and no resource requests. Without a readiness probe the Service sends traffic to a pod that is still booting; without requests the scheduler bin-packs blindly and the kubelet OOM-kills you. A manifest that applies cleanly but ships traffic to a not-ready pod is a latent incident, not a deployment.

kubernetes-manifests.text: A deploy goes out at 4:55 on a Friday, error rate triples, and the on-call opens the manifest to find `replicas: 3` and nothing else — no probe, no limit, no strategy. The pods are 'Running' and serving 500s, and there is no clean revision to roll back to because nobody declared one.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase of Cloud, DevOps, and Production Operations: you can build a container and push it through CI, but Kubernetes only deploys it as safely as the manifest tells it to. The manifest is the contract between your image and the cluster — it decides health, capacity, rollout, and reversibility.

kubernetes-manifests.prompt: Your pod shows STATUS `Running` and the Service is still routing traffic to it, but users get 500s. If the container process is up, why is the pod serving errors — and what single field would have kept traffic away until it was actually ready? Decide before reading.
kubernetes-manifests.reveal: `Running` means the container process started, not that the app can serve. Without a `readinessProbe`, the pod joins the Service Endpoints the instant the process is up — before the DB pool warms, config loads, or migrations finish — so the Service load-balances real traffic onto a booting pod. The readiness probe is the gate: a pod is only added to Endpoints once the probe passes. Liveness restarts a wedged pod; readiness decides whether it receives traffic at all. Confusing the two is the most common manifest bug in production.
