kubernetes-manifests.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
  labels: { app: orders }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: registry.internal/orders:1.8.2
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  selector: { app: orders }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
steps: revisionHistoryLimit — reversibility: Keeps the last 5 ReplicaSets so `kubectl rollout undo` has a last-good revision to return to. Set it to 0 and you have deleted your own rollback.
RollingUpdate: maxUnavailable 0: Never drop below full capacity during a rollout; add one surge pod at a time. maxUnavailable > 0 means you shed capacity mid-deploy — exactly when load may spike.
The selector must match the Pod labels: The Service and Deployment both select `app: orders`. A label typo silently orphans pods — the Service selects nothing and returns no endpoints.

Resource requests + limits: requests drive scheduling (the node reserves 250m/256Mi); limits cap blast radius (the kubelet OOM-kills at 512Mi instead of taking the node down). Omit requests and the scheduler bin-packs blindly.

readinessProbe — the traffic gate: The pod only joins the Service Endpoints once /healthz/ready returns 200. This is the field the pretest incident was missing: it keeps the Service from load-balancing onto a booting pod.

livenessProbe — the restart gate: A separate path with a longer initialDelay so a slow boot is not mistaken for a wedge. Liveness restarts; readiness withholds traffic. Different jobs, different endpoints.
The Service fronts the pods: One stable virtual IP; it load-balances only across Ready pods. targetPort 8080 hits the container; port 80 is what callers dial.

kubernetes-manifests.title: The rollout path — and the two paths a bad revision can take
kubernetes-manifests.subtitle: kubectl apply drives the Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. The readiness probe gates the Service; a failing rollout either heals (rollout undo) or, unguarded, poisons live traffic. Ingress, secrets, and the DB are out of scope for this manifest.

legend.label: the bad revision the probe is meant to catch

storyboard.say: It starts with kubectl apply — you hand the cluster a manifest, the desired end state it will work to make true.
The Deployment reads that spec and creates a new ReplicaSet — the controller responsible for holding your target replica count.
The ReplicaSet schedules Pods onto nodes. They flip to Running fast — but Running only means the process started, not that it's healthy.
The readiness probe is the gate: a Pod joins the Service's Endpoints and takes live traffic only once it actually reports Ready.
Now the risk. Roll a bad revision and the strategy's surge exposes it — replacing old pods with new ones that shouldn't be trusted yet.
With a readiness probe, failing pods never gate into the Service, the rollout halts, and rollout undo reverts to the last good revision.
Without those fields, Running pods serve 500s and there's nothing to revert to. Every field the SLO needs must be declared, or Kubernetes picks a worse default.

kubernetes-manifests.question: Reviewer challenge: your Deployment applied cleanly, `kubectl get pods` shows all pods `Running`, yet the Service is returning 500s to users. What is the most likely manifest defect?
options: The replicas count is too low, so the pods are overloaded.
There is no readinessProbe, so pods join the Service Endpoints before the app can actually serve — the Service load-balances onto booting pods.
The image tag is wrong, so the wrong version deployed.
The Service uses the wrong port number, so no traffic arrives at all.
kubernetes-manifests.explanation: `Running` is a container-process state, not an application-ready state. Without a readinessProbe, Kubernetes adds the pod to the Service Endpoints the moment the process is up, so the Service happily routes real traffic to a pod that is still booting — producing 500s. (A wrong port (4) would drop ALL traffic, not return 500s from Running pods; a wrong tag (3) would fail differently; low replicas (1) causes latency, not immediate errors.)

storyboard.say: IaC keeps three things in sync: your Terraform code declares what you want, and it flows toward the live cloud.
terraform plan is the referee. It reads three inputs to decide what changes.
Code says desired, the state file says what was last recorded, and a refresh reads the actual live cloud.
When they match, apply reconciles: plan pushes the desired shape into the cloud and updates state.
Now the 3 a.m. failure: on-call opens the console and bumps instance count, bypassing the code entirely.
That out-of-band edit forks actual away from code and creates drift the code never knows about.
The next unrelated apply overwrites the console fix, because plan sees code, not the manual change.
The repair: plan detects the drift, then import plus re-apply pulls it back into code. Invariant: no out-of-band changes.

A reviewer can start from the metric spike, jump to the trace, land on the log line, and reach the same root cause you did — without you narrating.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.doNotClaim: Do not claim observability from three disconnected dashboards. Logs you cannot join to a trace, and a metric that says "errors up" but cannot tell you WHERE, is monitoring, not observability. If you cannot pivot metric → trace → log on one shared id, you have three silos, not a debuggable system.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.text: 12:04 — you ship v2.3. 12:07 — checkout error rate crosses the SLO and the page fires. The dashboard screams "5xx up 8x" but not WHERE, six services deep. The engineer who rolls back in four minutes has one trace_id that walks the request from gateway to the exact span that broke; the one still grepping raw pods at 12:40 has logs but nothing to join them on.

A deploy under production pressure fails in a distributed system you cannot fully see. Logs, metrics, and traces are the three signals that turn "something is wrong" into "this span, in this service, since this rollout" — this lesson's packet is the artifact you carry into the incident drill and the capstone readiness review.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.prompt: Errors spike right after a deploy. You have logs, metrics, AND traces all wired up. Which do you open FIRST — and why does the order matter? Decide before reading.
observability-logs-metrics-traces.reveal: Metric first, then trace, then log — and the order is the whole skill. The metric (error rate / latency SLO) tells you SOMETHING broke and roughly when; it is cheap and always-on. The trace tells you WHERE — which span in which service owns the failure. The log tells you WHY — the exception, the bad value, the config. Open logs first and you are grepping millions of lines with no coordinate system. The three are a funnel: metric narrows time, trace narrows place, log narrows cause. Observability is the ability to run that funnel on a shared trace_id — not owning three separate tools.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.intro: Instrumenting the payment span so it emits all three correlated signals. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
observability-logs-metrics-traces.code:
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics
import structlog

tracer = trace.get_tracer("payment-svc")
meter = metrics.get_meter("payment-svc")
charge_errors = meter.create_counter("payment_charge_errors_total")
charge_latency = meter.create_histogram("payment_charge_duration_ms")
log = structlog.get_logger()

def charge(order_id: str, amount_cents: int):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("payment.charge") as span:
        ctx = span.get_span_context()
        trace_id = format(ctx.trace_id, "032x")
        span.set_attribute("order.id", order_id)
        span.set_attribute("amount.cents", amount_cents)
        try:
            result = gateway.submit(order_id, amount_cents)   # v2.3 sends cents as string
            charge_latency.record(result.ms, {"outcome": "ok"})
            return result
        except GatewayError as e:
            span.record_exception(e)
            span.set_status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR)
            charge_errors.add(1, {"reason": e.code})
            log.error("charge_failed", trace_id=trace_id,
                      order_id=order_id, reason=e.code)
            raise
steps: Open the span (WHERE): start_as_current_span names payment.charge. Every downstream signal in this block now belongs to one node on the trace — this is the coordinate the whole funnel pivots on.
Extract the trace_id: Pull the 32-hex trace_id off the active span context. This single value is what will later join the log line back to this exact request — no shared id, no observability.
Attach span attributes: order.id and amount.cents become searchable trace facets. In the incident you filter traces by the failing order and land here directly.

The golden-signal metric — success path (WHEN): Record duration on every OK charge. Latency + the error counter below are the RED signals (Rate, Errors, Duration) that trip the SLO and tell you WHEN it started.
Mark the span failed: record_exception + StatusCode.ERROR make this span show up RED in the trace view — the reviewer sees the failing node at a glance, not a wall of green.

storyboard.say: A customer clicks buy. The request enters at the front door — ingress and gateway — the one place every checkout call must pass through.
The gateway mints a trace_id and hands off to checkout, stamping that same id onto every hop that follows.
Checkout fans out: it verifies the user against auth — healthy — then calls payment to charge the card.
Payment is throwing 500s. This is the break — the exact span, in the exact service, that the v2.3 deploy poisoned.
Every service emits its telemetry into one OTel collector — payment's failing span and checkout's spans and logs all funnel here.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.code:
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics
import structlog

tracer = trace.get_tracer("payment-svc")
meter = metrics.get_meter("payment-svc")
charge_errors = meter.create_counter("payment_charge_errors_total")
charge_latency = meter.create_histogram("payment_charge_duration_ms")
log = structlog.get_logger()

def charge(order_id: str, amount_cents: int):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("payment.charge") as span:
        ctx = span.get_span_context()
        trace_id = format(ctx.trace_id, "032x")
        span.set_attribute("order.id", order_id)
        span.set_attribute("amount.cents", amount_cents)
        try:
            result = gateway.submit(order_id, amount_cents)   # v2.3 sends cents as string
            charge_latency.record(result.ms, {"outcome": "ok"})
            return result
        except GatewayError as e:
            span.record_exception(e)
            span.set_status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR)
            charge_errors.add(1, {"reason": e.code})
            log.error("charge_failed", trace_id=trace_id,
                      order_id=order_id, reason=e.code)
            raise

steps.note: start_as_current_span names payment.charge. Every downstream signal in this block now belongs to one node on the trace — this is the coordinate the whole funnel pivots on.

steps.note: Pull the 32-hex trace_id off the active span context. This single value is what will later join the log line back to this exact request — no shared id, no observability.

steps.label: Attach span attributes
steps.note: order.id and amount.cents become searchable trace facets. In the incident you filter traces by the failing order and land here directly.

observability-logs-metrics-traces.text: DORA does tie delivery performance to fast recovery (failed-deployment recovery time is a core metric), but 'you cannot recover fast on a system you cannot see' is the author's observability assertion, not a DORA finding. Rewrite as: 'Standards grounding: DORA ties strong delivery performance to fast recovery (failed-deployment recovery time) — and in practice you cannot recover fast on a system you cannot see.' Two pro tells: (1) tail-based sampling (decide AFTER the request completes) keeps the erroring traces the head-sampler would have thrown away — the 1% you drop is exactly the 1% you need at 2 a.m. (2) Log cardinality is a cost bomb: put high-cardinality identifiers (order_id, trace_id) in structured FIELDS you can index and drop, not baked into the message string.

alerting-slo-error-budgets.outcome: Take one real service and define an SLO, compute its error budget, and write a MULTI-WINDOW BURN-RATE alert that pages only when the budget is being spent fast enough to matter — not on every blip. Package it as the alerting section of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.proof: Section of deployment_incident_repair_packet.md containing: one SLO (SLI + target + window), the derived error budget in minutes, and a Prometheus alerting rule with a fast burn-rate page and a slow burn-rate ticket. A reviewer can point to the exact PromQL, the rollout status, and a log/metric snapshot from a burn.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.unlock: Your alert fires on error-BUDGET burn rate over two windows — not on a raw threshold — and you can name the budget in minutes and what page vs ticket means.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have SLO alerting if your rule is 'alert when error rate > 1%'. A static threshold is not budget-aware: it pages at 3am for a harmless 2-minute spike and stays silent through a slow bleed that eats the whole month. The invariant is: alert on how fast the budget is being spent, over multiple windows.

alerting-slo-error-budgets.text: A deploy ships at 14:02. Errors tick from 0.1% to 0.9% — under every static threshold, so nothing pages. By 02:00 the month's error budget is gone, the SLO is breached, and the first anyone hears of it is a customer tweet. The alert that should have caught it was watching the wrong thing.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase of Cloud, DevOps, and Production Operations: you can already deploy, roll back, and read observability. Now you decide WHEN a human gets woken up — the SLO and its error budget turn 'is it broken?' into a measured, budget-aware page-or-ticket decision.

alerting-slo-error-budgets.prompt: Your SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days. Right now the service is returning errors on 5% of requests. Is this a page-someone-at-3am emergency? Decide before reading on.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.reveal: It depends entirely on how long it lasts — and that is the whole point. 99.9% over 30 days allows ~43 minutes of downtime (the error budget). A 5% error rate burns that budget ~50x faster than 'allowed': at that rate you exhaust the ENTIRE month in under an hour. THAT is the emergency — not the 5% number, but the burn RATE against a finite budget. A 5% blip lasting 20 seconds is noise; 5% sustained is a fire. A static '>1%' threshold cannot tell them apart.

alerting-slo-error-budgets.intro: The multi-window burn-rate alert, rule by rule. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.code:
groups:
- name: checkout-slo-burn
  rules:
  - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
    # 14.4x burn over 1h spends 2% of a 30d budget in 1h -> PAGE
    expr: |
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
      and
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout burning error budget 14.4x - budget gone in ~2 days"
  - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetSlowBurn
    # 3x burn over 6h spends ~5% of budget -> TICKET, not a 3am page
    expr: |
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate6h{job="checkout"} > (3 * 0.001)
      and
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate30m{job="checkout"} > (3 * 0.001)
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: ticket
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout slow error-budget bleed - investigate this shift"
steps: The fast-burn page: 14.4x is the standard SRE fast-burn multiplier: at that rate you spend 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. That earns a page.
TWO windows, ANDed: The 1h window catches the sustained burn; the 5m window confirms it is STILL burning right now. Both required -> a spike that already ended cannot page you.
for: 2m debounce: The condition must hold for 2 minutes before firing - kills the last of the flapping without meaningfully delaying a real fire.
severity: page: This label routes to the pager in Alertmanager. Slow burn below routes to a ticket queue instead - same signal, different urgency.
The slow-burn ticket: 3x burn over 6h is the silent bleed the intro described. It does not warrant a 3am wake-up, but it MUST be caught before it eats the month - so it files a ticket.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.commonMistake: Wrong both ways: noisy AND blind to the real breach

alerting-slo-error-budgets.title: From SLI to page: the error-budget burn path
alerting-slo-error-budgets.subtitle: The SLI feeds the budget; the burn-rate evaluator watches two windows. Fast burn on both -> page a human. Slow burn -> ticket. A brief spike burns one window only and is deliberately swallowed.

legend.label: budget + spikes we swallow on purpose

storyboard.say: Everything starts with the SLI — the live signal measuring what fraction of requests are actually succeeding right now.
The SLI is compared against the SLO target: 99.9% success over 30 days is the promise you've made.
One minus that target defines the error budget — the roughly 43 minutes of failure you're allowed to spend each month.
The burn-rate evaluator divides the live error ratio by the budget: actual failure over budgeted failure equals how fast you're burning.
When a short window AND a long window both show fast burn, the outage is real and sustained — page a human immediately.
A slow, steady bleed won't drain the budget tonight, so it files a ticket instead of waking anyone.
A brief spike lights the short window but leaves the long window cold — it's deliberately swallowed, no alert.
That two-window test is the whole point: static thresholds missed the slow 0.9% creep, but burn rate against the budget catches it.

alerting-slo-error-budgets.title: The multi-window burn-rate alert, rule by rule
alerting-slo-error-budgets.subtitle: A real Prometheus alerting rule for a 99.9%/30d SLO. Fast page (2% budget in 1h) requires BOTH a 1h and a 5m window; slow ticket (5% in 6h) requires 6h AND 30m.
alerting-slo-error-budgets.code:
groups:
- name: checkout-slo-burn
  rules:
  - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
    # 14.4x burn over 1h spends 2% of a 30d budget in 1h -> PAGE
    expr: |
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
      and
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m{job="checkout"} > (14.4 * 0.001)
    for: 2m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout burning error budget 14.4x - budget gone in ~2 days"
  - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetSlowBurn
    # 3x burn over 6h spends ~5% of budget -> TICKET, not a 3am page
    expr: |
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate6h{job="checkout"} > (3 * 0.001)
      and
      job:slo_errors:ratio_rate30m{job="checkout"} > (3 * 0.001)
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: ticket
    annotations:
      summary: "Checkout slow error-budget bleed - investigate this shift"

steps.label: The fast-burn page
steps.note: 14.4x is the standard SRE fast-burn multiplier: at that rate you spend 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. That earns a page.

steps.label: TWO windows, ANDed
steps.note: The 1h window catches the sustained burn; the 5m window confirms it is STILL burning right now. Both required -> a spike that already ended cannot page you.

steps.label: for: 2m debounce
steps.note: The condition must hold for 2 minutes before firing - kills the last of the flapping without meaningfully delaying a real fire.

steps.label: severity: page
steps.note: This label routes to the pager in Alertmanager. Slow burn below routes to a ticket queue instead - same signal, different urgency.

steps.label: The slow-burn ticket
steps.note: 3x burn over 6h is the silent bleed the intro described. It does not warrant a 3am wake-up, but it MUST be caught before it eats the month - so it files a ticket.

The two ANDed windows: the short window swallows an ended spike (long window stays cold), and the separate 6h/30m slow-burn rule catches the bleed the fast rule ignores.
The severity: page label routing to the pager.
The 14.4x multiplier being a large number.

A 30-second spike lights the 5m window briefly but never the 1h window, so the fast-burn AND is never true - swallowed. rollbacks-incident-response.outcome: Take a deployment that pushed elevated errors into production and drive the full recovery loop: detect against the SLO, roll back to the last good revision, instrument what you missed, and write the incident up. Produce the artifact deployment_incident_repair_packet.md — not a note, a reviewable packet with context, the chosen recovery, the rejected one, the expected failure, and the proof transcript.
rollbacks-incident-response.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger, backed by a kubectl transcript: `kubectl rollout status` before, `kubectl rollout undo` (or scaled traffic shift), rollout status after, an error-rate log excerpt, and a metric snapshot showing the SLO recovering. A reviewer can point to the exact line that proves errors fell after rollback.
rollbacks-incident-response.unlock: Your packet names the SLO breach that triggered rollback, shows the rollout undone to a known-good revision with proof it recovered, and records what instrumentation you added so the next bad deploy is caught faster.
rollbacks-incident-response.doNotClaim: Do not claim an incident was 'resolved' because you rolled back. Rollback stops the bleeding; it does not explain the wound. A packet with no autopsy of WHY the deploy shipped bad — no failing signal, no added instrumentation — is a mute button, not incident response. The invariant: every rollback ends with a control that makes the same failure louder or impossible next time.

rollbacks-incident-response.text: 2:14 a.m. The deploy went green, then checkout 500s climb from 0.2% to 9% and the SLO burn alert fires. One engineer starts reading the new code line by line; the other types `kubectl rollout undo` and has traffic healthy in ninety seconds — then goes hunting for why. Only one of them is doing incident response.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase of Cloud, DevOps, and Production Operations: you can already ship a Kubernetes deployment with health checks — now you must survive shipping a bad one. Rollback is the reversibility that makes fast deploys safe, and the incident packet is the evidence that turns a 2 a.m. scramble into an auditable, repeatable control.

rollbacks-incident-response.prompt: A deploy just spiked your error rate past the SLO. Your instinct is to read the diff and hotfix forward. Why is 'roll back first' almost always the better first move? Answer before reading on.
rollbacks-incident-response.reveal: Because rollback and diagnosis are different jobs, and only one is on the clock. Rolling forward means writing, reviewing, building, and deploying NEW untested code while the incident burns — you are debugging in production under maximum pressure, the worst possible conditions. Rollback returns you to a revision you already proved good, which stops user-facing harm AND buys you calm, offline time to find the real cause. Mean-time-to-recovery, not mean-time-to-understand, is what the SLO measures. You restore first, then you get to be curious.

rollbacks-incident-response.intro: The rollback transcript that becomes your proof. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
rollbacks-incident-response.code:
# 1. Confirm the SLO breach is real and tied to THIS rollout
kubectl rollout status deploy/checkout        # "1 of 4 updated... " revision 47 live
kubectl logs deploy/checkout --since=5m | grep -c ' 500 '   # 5xx count: 812 (was ~5)

# 2. See the revision history — what is the last known-good?
kubectl rollout history deploy/checkout       # rev 46 = last healthy, rev 47 = bad

# 3. Restore service: roll back to the previous good revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/checkout --to-revision=46

# 4. Watch the rollback land, then re-check the error signal
kubectl rollout status deploy/checkout        # "successfully rolled out"
kubectl logs deploy/checkout --since=2m | grep -c ' 500 '   # 5xx count: 3 — recovered
steps: Detect, do not assume: Tie the SLO burn to this rollout before you touch anything. Revision 47 is live; the 5xx count jumped from ~5 to 812. That grep count is your first proof line.
Find the known-good revision: rollout history is the reason rollback is fast: Kubernetes keeps the previous ReplicaSet. Revision 46 was healthy — that is your target, not a fresh build.
Restore first with rollout undo: --to-revision=46 shifts pods back to the last good ReplicaSet. This is MTTR work: users recover in seconds, no new code compiled under pressure.

Verify recovery is the proof: Rollback without verification is hope. rollout status confirms the revision landed; the second grep (5xx back to 3) is the metric snapshot that PROVES the SLO recovered. This line is what the reviewer points to.

storyboard.say: 2:14 a.m. A new deploy rolls out to the Service pods, and ingress keeps sending real checkout traffic straight at it.
The pods emit climbing 5xx into Observability — checkout errors race from 0.2% to 9% and the SLO burn alert fires.
Now the fork: read the new code line by line, or restore service first. The reversible move wins — decide to revert.
kubectl rollout undo swaps the bad revision back to the last known-good one — traffic is healthy again in ninety seconds.
Only after service is restored do you go hunting: the autopsy asks why the alert didn't catch this sooner.
The autopsy leaves a louder signal behind in Observability, so the next bad deploy trips a sharper wire.
The invariant: recovery before understanding, and every rollback leaves a new alarm — that closed loop is incident response.

Rewrite as: 'This is grounded in DORA: elite teams score well on both stability metrics — change-failure rate and time-to-restore — not just one.' NIST AI RMF frames this under its 'Secure and Resilient' characteristic — resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event — so a system you cannot quickly return to a known-good state is a system you cannot responsibly operate. security-supply-chain.outcome: Take one real container service you ship and build the Security Supply Chain gate: generate an SBOM, attach signed provenance, and wire a CI/CD policy that BLOCKS an unsigned or critically-vulnerable image from reaching your Kubernetes cluster — then prove the gate rejects a bad artifact.
security-supply-chain.proof: The artifact `deployment_incident_repair_packet.md` with a supply-chain section: the SBOM path, the cosign signature + provenance attestation, the CI policy that fails the build on a CRITICAL CVE or missing signature, and a transcript showing the gate REJECT a tampered/unsigned image. A reviewer can trace one image from source commit to admission decision.
security-supply-chain.unlock: Your pipeline produces an SBOM, signs the image + provenance, and the admission gate provably refuses an artifact that fails either check.
security-supply-chain.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a 'secure supply chain' because you added a vulnerability scanner that only WARNS. A scanner whose findings never fail the build is a dashboard, not a gate. The invariant is enforcement: an untrusted artifact must be unable to reach production, not merely annotated.

security-supply-chain.text: 3 a.m. page: a dependency you never chose — pulled in five levels deep by a transitive `npm install` — shipped a backdoor, and it is already running in your cluster. The room asks the one question that decides the blast radius: 'What is actually inside the image we deployed, and can we prove nobody swapped it?' If you cannot answer from an SBOM and a signature, you are reading the source of a container you can no longer trust.

This lesson sits in the synthesis phase of Cloud, DevOps & Production Operations: it fuses containers, CI/CD, and Kubernetes admission into one trust boundary. The Security Supply Chain is the artifact-integrity layer — everything BETWEEN your source commit and a running pod — where SolarWinds-class attacks live and where a signed, inventoried image is the only defensible proof.

security-supply-chain.prompt: Your CI runs Trivy on every image and posts the CVE count to the PR. A teammate says 'we scan every build, our supply chain is secure.' Before reading on — what is still wide open?
security-supply-chain.reveal: Scanning proves what KNOWN vulnerabilities are inside; it proves nothing about WHO built the artifact or whether it was swapped after the scan. The two silent gaps: no provenance (an attacker who compromises the registry replaces the scanned image with a malicious one — same tag, same scan record) and no enforcement (findings that only post to the PR never stop a merge). Integrity and enforcement are different axes from detection — and the SolarWinds attack passed every vulnerability scan, because the malware was signed by the vendor's own compromised build system.

security-supply-chain.intro: The CI/CD supply-chain gate, one step at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
security-supply-chain.code:
jobs:
  secure-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write        # OIDC → keyless cosign signing
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Generate SBOM (CycloneDX)
        run: syft ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }} -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
      - name: Scan — FAIL on CRITICAL
        run: trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Push image
        run: docker push ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Sign image (keyless, OIDC identity)
        run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Attest SBOM as provenance
        run: cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.json \
               --type cyclonedx ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
steps: Keyless identity, not a stored key: id-token: write lets cosign sign with the workflow's OIDC identity via Sigstore/Fulcio — no long-lived signing key to leak. The signer's identity (the repo + workflow) is baked into the certificate.

SBOM: the inventory: syft walks every layer and emits a CycloneDX bill of materials — every package and transitive dependency. This is what answers '3 a.m.: what is actually inside?' in seconds instead of hours.

--exit-code 1 is the whole lesson: Without this flag Trivy prints CVEs and returns 0 — a warning. With it, a CRITICAL finding fails the job and the image never pushes. Detection became a GATE on one flag.
Sign the image: cosign attaches a signature tied to the OIDC identity. The admission gate later verifies THIS — proving the image was built by your pipeline, not swapped in the registry.

Attest the SBOM as provenance: The signed attestation binds the inventory to the image digest. Now 'what is inside' and 'who built it' are both cryptographically verifiable at admission — the two gaps the pretest exposed.

security-supply-chain.subtitle: Source → build → sign → registry → admission. The green path carries an SBOM + provenance the gate verifies. Two red edges show where trust breaks: a poisoned dependency enters at build, and a swapped image enters at the registry. The Kyverno/Sigstore gate is the last line — an unsigned or CRITICAL-CVE image is REJECTED, never scheduled.

legend.label: attack path the gate must stop

storyboard.say: It starts here: a commit in your source repo triggers the CI build. This is the entry to the supply chain.
But CI also pulls dependencies. Five levels deep, a transitive npm install drags in a poisoned package you never chose.
CI does its job right: it pushes a signed image plus an SBOM inventory into the registry.
Second attack path: an attacker swaps the image in the registry under the same tag, so the digest changes but the name looks identical.
On deploy, the registry hands the image to the admission gate as a pull request. This is the last checkpoint.
The Kyverno and Sigstore gate verifies the signature and scans the SBOM. Signature valid, no critical CVE, so the pod is admitted.
A swapped or unsigned image fails signature check; a critical CVE fails the scan. Either way the gate rejects it back at the registry.
The invariant: an unverifiable artifact cannot run. Detection without enforcement is theater; the gate is what makes proof binding.

        run: docker push ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Sign image (keyless, OIDC identity)
        run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Attest SBOM as provenance
        run: cosign attest --yes --predicate sbom.json \
               --type cyclonedx ghcr.io/acme/orders:${{ github.sha }}

steps.label: Keyless identity, not a stored key
steps.note: id-token: write lets cosign sign with the workflow's OIDC identity via Sigstore/Fulcio — no long-lived signing key to leak. The signer's identity (the repo + workflow) is baked into the certificate.

steps.label: SBOM: the inventory
steps.note: syft walks every layer and emits a CycloneDX bill of materials — every package and transitive dependency. This is what answers '3 a.m.: what is actually inside?' in seconds instead of hours.

steps.label: --exit-code 1 is the whole lesson
steps.note: Without this flag Trivy prints CVEs and returns 0 — a warning. With it, a CRITICAL finding fails the job and the image never pushes. Detection became a GATE on one flag.

steps.label: Sign the image
steps.note: cosign attaches a signature tied to the OIDC identity. The admission gate later verifies THIS — proving the image was built by your pipeline, not swapped in the registry.

steps.label: Attest the SBOM as provenance
steps.note: The signed attestation binds the inventory to the image digest. Now 'what is inside' and 'who built it' are both cryptographically verifiable at admission — the two gaps the pretest exposed.

DORA's research links security/software-supply-chain capabilities to performance, but the specific claims 'enforce artifact integrity ship MORE' and 'removes the manual review fear-tax' are the author's causal framing, not stated DORA findings; the 2024 report notably found AI adoption correlated with a stability drop. Rewrite as: 'DORA\'s research associates secure software-supply-chain practices with stronger delivery performance; in practice, teams that enforce artifact integrity can ship confidently because a trusted pipeline removes the manual-review fear-tax.'

security-supply-chain.question: Reviewer challenge: 'Show me the exact evidence this stops a real attack, not just a happy-path demo.' Which artifact-plus-proof combination actually demonstrates an enforced supply chain?
options: A Trivy report attached to the PR showing zero CRITICAL CVEs at merge time.
An SBOM committed to the repo plus a screenshot of a green build.
A cosign-signed image with an SBOM attestation, PLUS a transcript where the admission gate REJECTS an unsigned copy of the same image (same tag, no signature) with ImagePullBackOff / policy denied.
A signed image and a passing scan, deployed successfully to the cluster.
security-supply-chain.explanation: Only option 3 proves ENFORCEMENT against the actual threat: the swapped/unsigned artifact is refused at admission. A clean scan (1) proves detection at one moment but not integrity or that anything blocks. An SBOM + green build (2) is inventory without a gate. A successful deploy of a good image (4) is the happy path — it never shows the gate saying 'no', which is the only evidence that matters.

left.label: Scan-and-hope

No SBOM — 'what's inside?' takes hours of grep

K8s pulls whatever the registry serves for that tag
A swapped image with the same tag deploys silently
left.verdict: Detection theater — nothing is actually blocked

right.label: Inventory + provenance + enforced gate
lines: trivy --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL fails the build
syft SBOM attested + signed to the image digest
cosign keyless signature (OIDC identity, no stored key)
Kyverno verifyImages requires a valid signature to admit
Unsigned or CRITICAL image → ImagePullBackOff, never runs

Re-tag a malicious image over a trusted tag in a scratch registry and show the signature verification fails — proving tag mutation is caught, not trusted.

A reviewer can see WHERE the money goes and WHY the cut is safe.

cost-capacity-finops.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'reduced cost' if all you did was shrink replicas until something got cheaper. Cost without a defended SLO floor is not FinOps — it is deferred incident. The number that proves the work is cost-per-request AT the reliability target, not raw spend.

cost-capacity-finops.text: Finance forwards the cloud bill: the orders service costs $9,400/month and traffic hasn't grown in a quarter. The VP says 'cut it in half by Friday.' Someone reaches for --replicas=3, and the staff engineer asks the one question that stops the room: 'Half of what — and what breaks at p99 when you do?'

This is the synthesis lesson of Cloud, DevOps & Production Operations: it fuses everything before it — containers, Kubernetes, rollout, observability, incidents — into the decision that funds the platform. Cost and capacity is where reliability, unit economics, and reversibility collide, and where a careless save becomes next week's outage.

cost-capacity-finops.prompt: A service costs $9,400/month. Is that number enough to decide what to cut? Answer before reading on.
cost-capacity-finops.reveal: No — total spend is a vanity number. It hides whether you are paying for traffic or for idle. The unit that decides is cost-per-request: $9,400 over 47M requests is $0.0002/req, and if 70% of pods sit at 12% CPU, you are buying idle, not throughput. Cut the idle (right-size + autoscale), never the SLO. 'Cut it in half' framed as raw dollars quietly decides you will trade reliability for the invoice.

cost-capacity-finops.intro: The right-sizing artifact: requests, limits, and an HPA with a floor. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
cost-capacity-finops.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m      # was 1000m — pods idled at 12% of a full core
    memory: 512Mi  # was 1Gi   — RSS peaked at 340Mi over 30d
  limits:
    cpu: 750m      # headroom for bursts, not 4x the request
    memory: 768Mi
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  minReplicas: 3         # reliability floor — never scale below quorum
  maxReplicas: 20        # ceiling caps the blast radius on a traffic spike
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60   # scale out before p99 degrades, not after
steps: Right-size the request: The request is what the scheduler reserves and what you PAY for. Pods idled at 12% of a full core, so 1000m was buying idle. 250m is set from the observed p95 of actual usage, not a guess.
Limits ≠ 4× the request: A limit far above the request invites noisy-neighbor CPU throttling and OOM surprises. Set the limit to real burst headroom (measured), so the change is safe, not just cheap.
minReplicas is the SLO floor: This is the line that makes the cut reversible-safe: never scale below quorum (3) no matter how quiet traffic gets. Cost bottoms out here; reliability does not.
maxReplicas caps the bill's blast radius: A spike (or a retry storm) can autoscale you into a surprise invoice. The ceiling bounds cost the way the floor bounds reliability.

Target 60% util — scale BEFORE pain: Scaling at 60% CPU leaves headroom to add pods before p99 climbs. Target 90% and the autoscaler reacts after the SLO is already breaching. This is the knob that trades cost against latency safety.

cost-capacity-finops.question: Committed-use discounts: how much of your baseline do you lock in?

optionA.label: Reserve 100% at the current baseline
optionA.text: Max discount (~50% off on-demand), but you pre-pay for capacity you may not need — and a right-sizing win you make next month is now sunk cost you cannot give back for 1–3 years.

optionB.label: Reserve ~60% (the steady floor), burst on-demand
optionB.text: Slightly less discount, but the commitment matches load you are certain of. You keep the freedom to right-size the variable top layer and capture those savings too.

cost-capacity-finops.guidance: Reserve the floor you are confident in AFTER right-sizing, not the fat baseline you are about to trim. Committing to waste for three years is the most expensive 'saving' in FinOps. B keeps optionality; only reach for A once the workload is proven flat and already right-sized.

cost-capacity-finops.title: The FinOps loop: measure → attribute → right-size → guard
cost-capacity-finops.subtitle: Bill and metrics feed cost-per-request; the idle is right-sized and handed to autoscaling; the SLO guard can veto or roll back the cut. The failure path (cut breaches p99) and the repair path (roll back / raise the floor) are both drawn.

legend.label: SLO guard — the cut's failure + repair path

storyboard.say: The cloud bill lands: this service costs $9,400 a month. Before anyone touches replicas, we turn that dollar figure into a rate.
Cost-per-request fuses the bill as numerator with usage metrics as denominator — spend per unit of work, the only number that survives scrutiny.
Now attribute the idle: where is the waste? Traffic is flat, so we find the capacity we're paying for but not using.
Right-size cuts the idle, not the throughput — we trim the slack we proved was there, not the headroom that serves real load.
The trimmed footprint is handed to the autoscaler, which now runs the service under real production load.
The SLO guard watches under load. The reliability floor is fixed first — if the cut breaches p99, the guard vetoes it.
On breach we roll back and raise the floor, then retry the right-size. A cut that breaks the SLO is not a saving.

multi-env-promotion.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) service and design its multi-environment promotion path — dev → staging → prod — as a gated pipeline where the SAME artifact is promoted, each gate is a machine check, and a failed promotion rolls back to the last-known-good on its own. Then break it and write the incident autopsy.
multi-env-promotion.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md with a promotion section: the immutable artifact ID, the ordered gates (build → staging health → prod canary), the auto-rollback trigger, plus a kubectl rollout transcript and one metric snapshot showing a bad promotion was caught before full traffic. A reviewer can point to the exact gate that stopped it.
multi-env-promotion.unlock: Your pipeline promotes ONE immutable artifact across all three environments, every gate can fail and halt promotion, and a failed prod step rolls back automatically to the previous revision.
multi-env-promotion.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'multi-env promotion' if each environment rebuilds the image from source. Rebuilding per environment means staging and prod ran DIFFERENT binaries — you tested one thing and shipped another. That is deploy-three-times, not promote-one-artifact, and it is the exact failure this skill exists to kill.

multi-env-promotion.text: A deploy goes green in staging, so it ships straight to prod — and error rates triple at 2 a.m. because staging rebuilt a different image than prod did. The on-call engineer who promoted the SAME digest through a canary gate never gets paged; the one who 'just redeployed to prod' spends the night rolling back by hand.

This is the synthesis lesson: containers, CI/CD, Kubernetes, rollout, and observability converge here. Promotion is the discipline that turns 'it worked on my machine' into 'the byte-identical artifact that passed staging is the one now serving prod traffic behind a health gate.'

multi-env-promotion.prompt: Staging is green, so you promote to prod by running the build pipeline again against the prod branch. What is the hidden bug in that plan — before a single request fails? Answer first.
multi-env-promotion.reveal: You never actually tested what you shipped. A rebuild pulls fresh base layers, re-resolves dependency ranges, and can bake a different digest — so 'staging passed' certifies a binary that no longer exists. Real promotion moves ONE immutable artifact (a pinned image digest, e.g. app@sha256:9f2c…) untouched through every environment. The environment changes via config and secrets injected at deploy time; the artifact never does. Rebuilding per env is the silent source of 'passed staging, broke prod.'

multi-env-promotion.intro: The promotion pipeline, one stage at a time. Trace the complete operator artifact before implementing its deterministic decision model.
multi-env-promotion.code:
# promote.yml — promote ONE immutable artifact dev -> staging -> prod
IMAGE="registry.example.com/orders@sha256:9f2c4d..."   # pinned by DIGEST, not :latest

# 1. STAGING: deploy the exact digest + staging config, then gate on health
kubectl -n staging set image deploy/orders orders=$IMAGE
kubectl -n staging rollout status deploy/orders --timeout=120s   # gate: fails -> job fails

# 2. PROD CANARY: same digest, 5% of traffic, watch the SLO for 5 min
kubectl -n prod set image deploy/orders-canary orders=$IMAGE
ERR=$(promtool query instant $PROM 'rate(http_5xx[5m]) / rate(http_total[5m])')
if (( $(echo "$ERR > 0.02" | bc -l) )); then           # gate: error-rate > 2% SLO
  kubectl -n prod rollout undo deploy/orders-canary     # AUTO-ROLLBACK to last-known-good
  echo "canary breached SLO ($ERR) — promotion halted"; exit 1
fi

# 3. PROMOTE TO FULL: only the digest that survived the canary reaches 100%
kubectl -n prod set image deploy/orders orders=$IMAGE
kubectl -n prod rollout status deploy/orders --timeout=180s
steps: Pin by digest, never :latest: sha256:9f2c… is the whole discipline — this exact byte string is promoted through every environment. A tag like :latest is mutable and can point at a different image tomorrow.
Staging is a gate, not a checkpoint: rollout status blocks until the new pods are Ready; a failed rollout fails the job and stops promotion. Staging config differs, the artifact does not.
The prod canary gate: Send the SAME digest to 5% of traffic and read the live SLO (5xx error rate). This is where a bad artifact is caught with blast radius capped at 5%.
Auto-rollback on breach: rollout undo restores the previous revision with no human in the loop. The pipeline can only go back or forward — never leave prod half-broken.
Only survivors reach 100%: Full promotion runs only after the canary held the SLO. The digest at 100% is provably the one that passed staging AND the canary — no rebuild in between.

multi-env-promotion.title: The promotion pipeline — one artifact, three gates, an auto-rollback path
multi-env-promotion.subtitle: Build once → promote the SAME image digest dev → staging → prod. Each gate is a health/SLO check that can halt promotion. The prod canary gate is where a bad artifact is caught; failure routes to automatic rollback, never forward.

legend.label: the one immutable artifact, promoted untouched

storyboard.say: It starts with one build. CI compiles the code once and pushes an immutable image, pinned by its content digest, into the registry.
That exact digest promotes into dev. Not a rebuild — the same bytes, so what you test is literally what shipped.
The same artifact moves to the staging gate, which runs a health and SLO check that must pass or promotion simply halts.
On pass, the identical digest reaches the prod canary gate — the last checkpoint before real traffic, watching error rates and SLOs.
If the canary's SLOs hold, promotion completes and the digest ramps to one hundred percent of prod traffic.
But an error-rate breach never routes forward. The canary trips and hands off to automatic rollback.
Rollback restores the previous known-good revision in prod — no 2 a.m. page, no scramble, just the last artifact that passed.
The insight: build once, pin by digest, promote THAT through gates. Config changes per env; the artifact never does.

multi-env-promotion.text: Elite performers are defined across all four/five metrics, not just deployment frequency and change-failure rate; and 'promoting one small immutable artifact behind automated gates' is an implementation technique DORA does not prescribe (DORA does note reducing batch size helps). Rewrite as: 'DORA\'s elite performers score well across all the key metrics — throughput and stability together — and DORA notes reducing batch size improves them; promoting one small, immutable artifact behind automated gates is a practical way to do that.' NIST AI RMF frames the related idea under 'Accountable and Transparent' and provenance: you should be able to prove which exact version is in production and reverse it fast. (Note: the RMF does not use the word 'traceability'; it uses 'provenance' and accountability/transparency.) The senior tell is that their rollback path is code that runs on a breach, not a runbook step someone remembers to do.

multi-env-promotion.question: A reviewer asks for the ONE piece of evidence that proves your promotion pipeline is safe, not just green. Which do you point to?
options: The staging environment showing all tests passing before release.
A kubectl rollout transcript plus a metric snapshot where the prod canary gate detected an SLO breach and auto-rollback restored the previous revision — while the promoted digest matched staging's.
A screenshot of the CI pipeline with a green checkmark on every stage.
The Dockerfile showing the image builds successfully.
multi-env-promotion.explanation: Only option 2 proves the properties that matter: the SAME digest crossed environments (no rebuild drift), a gate could and did say 'no', and rollback happened automatically. Green staging (1), a green pipeline (3), and a building Dockerfile (4) all show the happy path — none of them demonstrate that a bad promotion gets caught and reversed, which is the entire point of the skill.

A reviewer who has never seen your service can restate its rollback path and its SLO from the packet alone.
production-readiness-review.unlock: Your packet names the rollout strategy, the exact rollback command, the health probe, the SLO the telemetry watches, and the runbook step for the feared failure — each with evidence, none as a promise.
production-readiness-review.doNotClaim: Do not claim a service is 'production ready' because it deploys green. Green on deploy is the happy path. Readiness is proven by the FAILURE path: show the rollback ran, the probe caught a bad pod, and the alert fired. A checklist with no failure evidence is theater.

production-readiness-review.text: A deploy ships Friday at 4pm, error rate climbs from 0.1% to 6%, and the on-call opens the runbook to find one line: 'roll back if needed.' No command, no health check that caught it, no SLO that alerted — just three engineers guessing while customers get 500s.

This is the synthesis lesson of the Cloud, DevOps, and Operations course: it pulls containers, Kubernetes rollout, observability, incidents, and rollback into one gate you run before shipping. The Production Readiness Review is the artifact that turns 'it works on my machine' into 'it survives a bad deploy in front of real traffic.'

production-readiness-review.prompt: A service passes all its unit tests and the deploy goes green. Is it production ready? Answer before reading on.
production-readiness-review.reveal: No — you have only proven the happy path. Production readiness is about the paths tests do not cover: what happens when a pod fails its liveness probe, when the new rollout ships elevated errors, when latency blows the SLO at 2am. Green tests prove the code; a readiness review proves the OPERATION — rollout, rollback, health checks, telemetry, and a runbook someone can execute half-asleep. The tell of a junior review: it inspects the code. The tell of a senior review: it rehearses the failure.

production-readiness-review.code:
# Production Readiness Review — orders-api v2.4.0

## Context
- Service: orders-api (K8s deploy, 6 replicas, behind ingress)
- Change: new pricing logic; feared failure: elevated 5xx under real traffic

## Rollout (selected: canary)
- Strategy: canary 10% -> 50% -> 100%, 5 min soak each
- Proof: kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-api  ->  "successfully rolled out"

## Rollback (rejected: manual redeploy)
- Command: kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders-api --to-revision=41
- Proof: undo returns pods to image v2.3.0 in < 90s; last-good revision pinned

## Health checks
- readinessProbe: GET /healthz  (fails pod out of the ingress pool)
- livenessProbe: GET /livez     (restarts a wedged pod)
- Proof: kill a dependency -> probe fails -> pod removed from Endpoints

## Telemetry + SLO
- SLO: 5xx rate < 1% over 5 min; p99 latency < 400ms
- Alert: fires to on-call at 2x error budget burn
- Proof: metric snapshot at deploy; alert test fired in staging

## Runbook (feared failure: 5xx spike)
1. Confirm on dashboard (5xx panel)  2. kubectl rollout undo ...
3. Verify rollout status + 5xx recovers  4. Open incident, write autopsy

## Reviewer objection
- "Show the rollback actually worked" -> attached: undo transcript + recovery graph
steps: Context frames the feared failure: One sentence on the service and the specific failure you fear in production. 'Elevated 5xx under real traffic' is inspectable; 'something breaks' is not.
Rollout: strategy + proof command: Name the strategy (canary here) AND the command that proves it succeeded. 'kubectl rollout status' returning 'successfully rolled out' is the evidence, not a claim.

Rollback: the rejected option is named: Manual redeploy is the rejected approach — too slow under fire. The selected 'rollout undo --to-revision' pins the last-good revision. A rollback with no revision number is a hope.

Health checks catch the bad pod: readinessProbe pulls a bad pod OUT of the ingress pool so traffic never hits it; livenessProbe restarts a wedged one. Proof is killing a dependency and watching the pod leave Endpoints.
Telemetry ties to an SLO with a number: The SLO is the line the review defends: <1% 5xx, <400ms p99. The alert must have been TEST-FIRED, or the telemetry is decorative.

Runbook is an ordered, executable sequence: Numbered steps the on-call runs half-asleep at 2am — confirm, undo, verify, autopsy. 'Roll back if needed' is not a runbook; step 2 with the exact command is.

Reviewer objection is pre-answered with evidence: The packet anticipates 'prove the rollback worked' and attaches the undo transcript plus the recovery graph. This is what turns understood into usable.

production-readiness-review.title: The readiness gate: deploy path and the repair path it must prove
production-readiness-review.subtitle: Six components on the rollout → observe → decide loop. The happy path (green) ships; the failure path (warning) is the one the review actually certifies — probe catches the bad pod, SLO breach fires, rollback returns to the last-good revision.

legend.label: rollout + probes (does the deploy come up?)
failure path — SLO breach, page, rollback trigger
the safe state the review must prove reachable

storyboard.say: The gate starts in CI: a passing pipeline applies the manifest that tells Kubernetes to roll out the new revision.
The rollout doesn't get to serve on trust — every new pod must clear a health probe before it counts as ready.
On the happy path the probe passes, so ready pods take live traffic. This is the green route that ships.
But the review certifies the failure path: an unready pod is blocked at the probe and never reaches a customer.
Even good pods can go bad live — traffic emits telemetry, and the SLO monitor watches error rate against a real budget.
When the SLO breaches, two things fire at once: rollback triggers automatically, and the runbook pages the on-call.
Rollback restores the last-good revision through deploy — the loop closes and traffic is safe again.
The invariant: every control must have proof it FIRED — probe, SLO, rollback, runbook — not just a promise it exists.

production-readiness-review.text: DORA's research does show elite performers combine high throughput with short time-to-restore (speed and stability are not tradeoffs), but 'that comes from a rehearsed rollback, not a careful deploy' is the author's prescription, not a DORA finding. cloud-devops-capstone.outcome: Take one deployable service you own (or a realistic one) and assemble the full production slice — container, CI/CD gate, Kubernetes rollout, health checks, telemetry — then stage a bad deploy, roll it back with kubectl, and capture it all in deployment_incident_repair_packet.md: the decision, the rejected option, the proof transcript, the failure autopsy, and the transfer case.
cloud-devops-capstone.proof: deployment_incident_repair_packet.md attached to the evidence ledger, containing: (1) context + assumptions, (2) selected vs rejected rollout approach, (3) a kubectl rollout/rollback transcript proving reversibility, (4) a log excerpt + a metric/SLO snapshot showing the error spike and its recovery, (5) a post-incident review with one repair rule, and (6) the capstone connection. A reviewer traces the failing deploy to green without you narrating.
cloud-devops-capstone.unlock: Your packet shows a real service going bad and coming back — with health checks, a rollback transcript, an SLO snapshot, and one reusable repair rule, not just prose.
cloud-devops-capstone.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'operated a production service' if the only evidence is a green deploy. A happy-path rollout proves nothing about operability. The capstone is the rollback: no kubectl rollout undo transcript and no recovered SLO snapshot means the packet caps at 78 — you demonstrated deploy, not operations.

cloud-devops-capstone.text: v2.4 goes out at 4:58 p.m. on a Friday; by 5:03 the error rate is 12x baseline and the SLO burn alert is screaming. The engineer who shipped it is refreshing a dashboard in a panic — the engineer next to her types one command, watches the pods flip back to v2.3, and the graph falls to the floor. The difference between them is not talent. It is a rehearsed rollback path and the telemetry to know when to pull it.

This is the synthesis lesson of Course 05: every earlier skill — containerizing the app, gating it through CI/CD, deploying to the cloud, running it on Kubernetes, rolling it out safely, instrumenting it, drilling incidents, hardening it, and watching its cost — converges here into one deployable service you can prove you operate. The capstone win is not a working app; it is a reviewable incident-repair packet showing the service break and recover under your hands.

cloud-devops-capstone.prompt: A deploy just doubled your error rate. Your first instinct is to open the logs and find the root cause before doing anything. What does a seasoned operator do first — and why is 'debug first' the wrong opening move here?
cloud-devops-capstone.reveal: They roll back first, then debug. Mean-time-to-recovery is the metric that matters to users, not mean-time-to-understanding. A rollback is a two-way door — reversible, cheap, and it stops the bleeding in seconds; root-causing a live regression is a one-way commitment of the on-call's night while customers keep hitting 500s. 'Debug first' quietly optimizes for your curiosity over the SLO. The senior move: restore the last-known-good revision with `kubectl rollout undo`, confirm the metric recovers, and root-cause the bad image at leisure from the artifact you saved.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-service
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0        # never drop below 4 healthy pods
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: registry.internal/orders:v2.3
          readinessProbe:        # gate traffic until the pod can serve
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:         # restart a wedged pod
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
---
# --- incident transcript (paste into the packet) ---
$ kubectl set image deploy/orders-service orders=registry.internal/orders:v2.4
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-service        # 4/4 ready, but 5xx climbing
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders-service          # revert to prior revision
deployment.apps/orders-service rolled back
$ kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-service        # 4/4 ready on v2.3; SLO recovers
steps: maxUnavailable: 0 is the safety rail: Surge one new pod, retire an old one only after the new is Ready. A bad :v2.4 can never take capacity below the four healthy pods still serving v2.3 — the rollout stays reversible mid-flight.
Readiness gates traffic: Ingress sends requests only to pods that pass /healthz/ready. A pod that boots but cannot serve is held out — this is why a broken image degrades instead of hard-failing.
Liveness restarts the wedged: A pod that deadlocks gets killed and rescheduled. Readiness protects users; liveness protects the pod. Confusing the two is the classic operability bug.

The bad deploy: set image ships :v2.4. rollout status reports 4/4 Ready — the pods are healthy, but the application logic is wrong. Healthy pods are not a healthy service; only the SLO tells you that.
The one-command rollback: kubectl rollout undo reverts to the last revision without a rebuild or a redeploy pipeline. This transcript IS the reversibility proof the sprint-contract demands.
Confirm recovery on the metric: Do not stop at 'rolled back'. Re-check rollout status AND the SLO snapshot. Recovery is proven by the error rate falling, not by the command exiting 0.

cloud-devops-capstone.title: The assembled production slice — commit to recovery
cloud-devops-capstone.subtitle: Every Course 05 skill as one node on a single path: source → CI gate → registry → K8s rollout behind an Ingress → telemetry → the burn alert that triggers the rollback. The failure path (bad image → error spike) and the repair path (rollout undo → recovered SLO) are both marked.

legend.label: the repair path — the capstone proof

storyboard.say: It starts with one push. A commit hits the CI/CD gate — the last automated line of defense before anything reaches production.
The gate passes, publishes the image to the registry, and sets the deployment to v2.4 — Friday, 4:58 p.m.
Kubernetes gates pods on health checks, then the Ingress opens the door and starts serving live traffic.
Every request now emits signals into observability. This is where the story stops being a deploy and becomes an incident.
By 5:03 the error rate is 12x baseline. Telemetry crosses the SLO burn threshold and the alert triggers the rollback.
One command. Rollback undoes the deployment back to v2.3, the pods flip, and the error graph falls to the floor.
Operability is the invariant: the proof isn't the deploy — it's that a bad revision was detected by a signal and reversed by a command.
